Expose only BadgeAssignment→Door so the door policy scans every assignment.
Expose only Door→BadgeAssignments and derive a badge’s door from its printed label.

questions.prompt: The door policy starts with a Door and retrieves the current badge assignments for that door. Each Badge detail view must also reach its assigned Door. The badge directory answers holder-to-badge lookups separately, and assignment changes are committed through one service. Which navigation ends should the Door–BadgeAssignment link expose?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If publisher administration later needed to enumerate shipments by object traversal, add only that required inverse end and define how it stays consistent.
details.errorCorrection: Making every end bidirectional adds collections no client uses. A direct Shipment→Publisher edge duplicates a value reached through the pinned revision, and reversing the links breaks the required detail traversal.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Navigability expresses a model path a client traverses. A chain can support a display without adding a redundant shortcut or inverse collection.
details.scenarioApplication: Shipment detail follows its exact revision to the publisher. The admin searches by revision ID, and no described client traverses from Publisher or Revision to shipments.
details.transfer: For each association, list the actual client start and required path before deciding which ends need object navigation.

messages.text: The prompt names only two forward traversals; an inverse is not required merely because the domain relation can be reversed.
Publisher comes from the exact pinned revision; a direct Shipment→Publisher link duplicates that path and can drift.
Shipment detail begins with Shipment and follows Revision to Publisher, so the reversed paths do not satisfy it.

feedback.reason: The detail view requires two forward traversals; reverse searches already have indexed paths and no direct publisher shortcut is needed.

options.text: Expose Shipment→RouteRevision and RouteRevision→Publisher only; omit both inverse collections.
Expose all four directions because each association should be navigable from either object.
Add a direct Shipment→Publisher link and use it instead of the route revision path.
Expose only Publisher→RouteRevision and RouteRevision→Shipment, reversing the named client path.

questions.prompt: Each Shipment points to one exact RouteRevision, and a revision may serve many shipments. Shipment detail displays its publisher by traversing Shipment→RouteRevision→Publisher. Publisher administration searches revisions by ID; no client lists shipments from a revision or revisions from a Publisher. Which association ends should be navigable?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A room-keyed booking index could replace the inverse in-memory collection if the calendar no longer required direct traversal.
details.errorCorrection: Historical canceled booking records remain, but current room membership must still reflect the move rather than duplicate stale links.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The two clients require opposite traversals, while the atomic move operation owns inverse-link consistency.
details.scenarioApplication: Room calendar and Booking detail start at different ends; the move service updates both sides as one operation.
details.transfer: When a relationship changes endpoints, identify who updates every required navigable view.

messages.text: The calendar requires direct Room→Bookings traversal and no scan is offered.
Booking detail needs its exact current room link, not a display-name match.
A move changes the association; leaving the old link creates a stale room membership.

feedback.reason: The calendar starts at Room while booking detail starts at Booking, so each needs direct access to the other end. The move operation updates both memberships atomically, while canceled records remain historical.

options.text: Make Room–Booking navigable in both directions and update both links in the move operation.
Keep only Booking→Room and make the calendar search every booking.
Keep only Room→Booking and find the room for a booking by matching its displayed name.
Copy the booking into a new object on every move and leave the old room list unchanged.

questions.prompt: A room calendar traverses Room→Bookings to show all reservations. Each Booking detail also follows Booking→Room. A move operation updates the room link in both places atomically; canceled bookings remain in their own history. How should this relationship be navigable?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a policy admin screen had to inspect all bound exhibits without the registry, reverse navigation could be added.
details.errorCorrection: Sharing a policy does not make it necessary to store consumer objects on that policy.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A shared policy can be referenced by its consumers without carrying an inverse collection of every consumer.
details.scenarioApplication: Exhibit→Policy supports command checks; the policy registry owns policy lookup and does not need a back-reference.
details.transfer: For shared configuration, model the required consumer-to-version path and keep usage queries with their explicit index.

messages.text: The guard starts from Exhibit, so it must navigate to the policy; a reverse-only link cannot serve it.
Policy screens do not traverse to exhibits and the registry already answers that query.
A copied command list loses the identity of the policy version governing the exhibit.

feedback.reason: The command guard begins at Exhibit and needs its policy version; policy lookup is registry-backed, and policy screens do not enumerate exhibits. No stated client traverses from policy to consumers.

options.text: Expose Exhibit→MaintenancePolicy only.
Expose MaintenancePolicy→Exhibits only, so an exhibit can find its policy through the shared policy list.
Make it bidirectional and maintain the same exhibit collection already available from the policy registry.
Copy the policy’s current command list into Exhibit and store no policy reference.

questions.prompt: An exhibit object references its MaintenancePolicy to reject unsafe commands. The same policy version is shared by many exhibits. Policy screens never list exhibits, and the command guard starts from an exhibit. Which direction should the Exhibit–MaintenancePolicy association expose?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the domain introduced one separately defined current-destination value, a Shipment→CurrentHub association could be added for that distinct fact.
details.errorCorrection: One direct Hub loses earlier stops. A second hub collection duplicates event data and needs synchronization; Hub-to-Shipments is not needed because the repository already answers that query.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A navigable association should represent the path and granularity a client needs. A path through an event retains the event-specific relationship.
details.scenarioApplication: Each ScanEvent has one Hub, while a Shipment has many events at different Hubs. The shipment-level direct link would imply one Hub or duplicate a list derivable through its events.
details.transfer: When a relationship belongs to each event in a sequence, expose that event-level path instead of flattening it onto the aggregate.

messages.text: A Shipment visits multiple Hubs through different events, so one shipment-level Hub cannot represent every timeline stop.
The set of Hubs is already derived through the ScanEvents; storing it separately creates a second value to keep aligned.
Hub queries already use the indexed repository, and no model client needs an inverse collection.

feedback.reason: The timeline’s hub is event-specific; the existing event path preserves that distinction without a misleading shipment-level shortcut.

options.text: Expose Shipment→ScanEvents and ScanEvent→Hub; omit direct Shipment→Hub and Hub→Shipment links.
Store one direct Shipment→Hub link as the destination for every scan in its timeline.
Store a second Shipment→all-Hubs collection beside the ScanEvent links and update both on every scan.
Add Hub→Shipments collections so Hub screens can list shipments without the existing repository.

questions.prompt: A Shipment has many immutable ScanEvents, and each event names one Hub. Its timeline shows every visited Hub by traversing Shipment→ScanEvents→Hub; there is no single Hub for the whole Shipment. Hub search uses an indexed ScanRepository and keeps no shipment collection. Which navigation should the object model expose?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the timeline used an event-store query instead of object traversal, the Conversation-side collection could be removed.
details.errorCorrection: Do not confuse staff lookup with the Conversation–Event association; the directory serves that separate access path.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Both conversation-facing directions are required by named clients; other endpoints can remain query-backed.
details.scenarioApplication: Timeline and event detail traverse in opposite directions. The transaction maintains their paired references.
details.transfer: Model the minimum navigable ends per client while keeping distinct lookup routes separate.

messages.text: The staff directory already answers author queries; no author-side traversal is required.
The timeline requires direct Conversation→Events navigation.
Message text is not a stable reference to the exact conversation.

feedback.reason: The timeline starts at Conversation and event detail starts at EscalationEvent, so both paths have named consumers. The writer maintains them transactionally; staff lookup remains directory-backed.

options.text: Expose Conversation→EscalationEvents and EscalationEvent→Conversation; keep author search directory-backed.
Expose every end, including StaffMember→EscalationEvents, and duplicate the directory index.
Expose only Event→Conversation and scan all events for a conversation timeline.
Expose only Conversation→Events and derive an event’s conversation from message text.

questions.prompt: A conversation timeline traverses Conversation→EscalationEvents. Each event detail also follows EscalationEvent→Conversation. A timeline writer adds both links in one transaction; the staff directory provides author searches separately. Which ends of Conversation–EscalationEvent should be navigable?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the grant were only a transient unsaved preview with no audit obligation, deleting it on expiry could be appropriate.
details.errorCorrection: Do not confuse “no longer active” with “delete the object.” The case requires a retained lifecycle record.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An object can leave its active state without ending its record lifetime; audit retention is explicit here.
details.scenarioApplication: At the expiry instant, this Grant becomes expired and no longer authorizes access, while its ID and approval history remain stored.
details.transfer: When an object has both an active use period and a retention period, model those as separate lifecycle boundaries.

messages.text: Expiry removes authorization, but the prompt explicitly requires the grant record to remain auditable.
The scenario makes the grant’s expiry transition a domain responsibility, not a caller convention.
The role definition is shared and has a separate lifetime from any one grant.

feedback.reason: The grant must stop authorizing at expiry, but its retained ID and approval timestamps remain audit evidence. Expiring authority therefore does not mean deleting the grant record.

options.text: Expire the Grant’s authority but retain its audit record.
Delete the grant record at expiry and reconstruct it later from the role definition.
Leave the grant active and rely on every door caller to compare the expiry timestamp correctly.
Delete the shared role definition when this grant expires.

questions.prompt: A temporary access grant has a start and expiry instant. At expiry it stops authorizing access, but its grant ID, approver, and timestamps remain in the audit record. A role definition is shared by many grants. What lifecycle should the grant have when its expiry arrives?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the decisions were unsigned transient drafts, the system could discard them when the request is withdrawn.
details.errorCorrection: Do not model withdrawal as a destructive cascade when the facts require historical retrieval.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A parent workflow’s closed state can stop new child creation while preserving historical child records.
details.scenarioApplication: Withdrawal ends the request’s active review phase, not the persisted signed-decision records.
details.transfer: Separate the lifecycle of a workflow from the retention lifecycle of its already committed evidence.

messages.text: Signed decisions are explicitly retained after withdrawal; deletion would erase the required compliance history.
Withdrawal closes the decision process, so accepting new decisions violates the stated lifecycle boundary.
The request context is needed to identify which approval each decision belongs to.

feedback.reason: Withdrawal ends the opportunity to add decisions, while signed entries remain compliance evidence. Closing the request and retaining its committed decision records are separate lifecycle effects.

options.text: Close the request to new decisions; retain signed decision records.
Delete all reviewer decisions when the request is withdrawn.
Keep the request open for new decisions but hide the earlier signed records.
Move every decision into the current reviewer profile and remove its request context.

questions.prompt: A two-reviewer approval request stores each signed decision by reviewer and round. If the request is withdrawn, no new decision may be added, but earlier signed decisions must remain queryable for the compliance record. How should withdrawal affect the already recorded decisions?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If submission transferred the same draft objects into the durable inspection, the session could no longer delete them after commit.
details.errorCorrection: Do not attach the submitted record to the editor session merely because the editor created it.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Creation boundary separates temporary working state from the durable submitted record.
details.scenarioApplication: Cancel deletes the local drafts. Submit copies their values into a new Inspection that outlives the editor.
details.transfer: Identify whether a workflow commits the same object or creates a durable successor before assigning cleanup ownership.

messages.text: Before submission the drafts are session-local; after submission the durable Inspection is a separate object.
The prompt requires cancellation to remove local drafts, not retain them as permanent inspections.
One editor-session lifecycle owner can consistently remove its draft set.

feedback.reason: Cancel removes session-local drafts, whereas submit copies their values into a permanent Inspection that must outlive the editor. That copy creates a lifecycle boundary the editor cleanup cannot cross.

options.text: The editor owns its drafts; submit creates a separate Inspection.
Let the permanent Inspection own the drafts before submission and delete it whenever the editor closes.
Retain every canceled draft indefinitely as if it were a submitted inspection.
Have each section decide independently whether the editor session has ended.

questions.prompt: An inspection editor creates four local section drafts. Canceling the editor must remove those drafts. Submitting copies their values into a permanent Inspection record; later deleting the editor session must not affect the submitted record. Which object should control the local drafts’ lifetime?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If drafts were intentionally visible during editing, they should be modeled as a separate draft object with its own lifecycle.
details.errorCorrection: Do not publish a half-formed object and rely on each caller to clean up an invalid state.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The object’s creation boundary should coincide with the point at which its invariant is complete and publication is allowed.
details.scenarioApplication: Validation completes first; only successful publication creates the immutable Snapshot.
details.transfer: Create durable domain records at their declared commit point, and use a separate temporary representation for incomplete work.

messages.text: The case requires no partial snapshot to be visible on failed validation, so callers should not own compensating deletion.
The published snapshot’s input references are immutable, so mutation after publication violates the stated lifecycle.
Snapshot creation belongs to the publication event and depends on the validated full input set.

feedback.reason: Partial snapshots are prohibited, so validation is the creation boundary.

options.text: Create the immutable Snapshot only after validation succeeds.
Create a visible partial Snapshot first and let each caller remove it when validation fails.
Create the Snapshot before validating inputs and mutate its code reference after publication.
Have the code-version object create snapshots whenever any notebook references it.

questions.prompt: A notebook run creates an immutable result snapshot only after all input references validate. A failed publication attempt may be retried after repairing a missing code reference; no partial snapshot is visible before validation succeeds. When should the snapshot object be created?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If no replay detection were required after success, the whole challenge record could be removed immediately; this scenario explicitly requires the marker.
details.errorCorrection: Waiting for the deadline leaves a successfully used secret reusable. Deleting the account exceeds the challenge’s scope, and retaining an accepted secret defeats the one-time rule.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The challenge secret and its replay marker have separate lifecycle needs: the secret ends at successful use, while the consumed marker remains until the original expiry.
details.scenarioApplication: A second use must be rejected during the remaining 24-hour window; after expiry the challenge record can be purged without affecting the account or audit.
details.transfer: Separate credential material, replay evidence, and the identity whose access the credential protects when deciding what expires or is deleted.

messages.text: Successful confirmation consumes the one-time secret; leaving it usable permits the replay the prompt forbids.
The account and recovery audit are explicitly retained and are not owned by the temporary challenge.
Expiry is the fallback lifetime limit, but successful use invalidates the secret earlier.

feedback.reason: Confirmation consumes the one-time secret, but its marker remains to reject replay until the original expiry. The account and recovery audit have separate lifetimes from that challenge state.

options.text: Consume the secret on success; retain its replay marker until expiry.
Keep the challenge usable until its 24-hour expiry so a repeated confirmation can succeed again.
Delete the account and its recovery audit when the challenge is consumed.
Retain and accept the same secret after success, using the expiry as the only replay control.

questions.prompt: An account recovery challenge contains a one-time secret and has a fixed expiry 24 hours after issue. Successful confirmation must make the secret unusable immediately. The system keeps a consumed challenge marker until that original expiry to reject replay, then may purge the marker; the account and recovery audit remain. What lifecycle should confirmation trigger?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the server stored the same remote object by reference rather than creating a separate durable record, the cleanup contract would have to change.
details.errorCorrection: Avoid treating copied draft data as one object shared across device and server lifetimes.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A copy-and-acknowledge boundary gives the temporary queue and committed server object separate lifetimes.
details.scenarioApplication: The queue keeps the local draft until acknowledgement, then removes that local object; the server Inspection remains.
details.transfer: Tie cleanup of temporary copies to the explicit commit/acknowledgement boundary.

messages.text: The server creates a separate durable record, so acknowledged local copies may be removed without deleting that record.
Deleting before acknowledgement can lose the only copy if submission fails.
The scenario distinguishes temporary device drafts from the durable server record; it does not require permanent local copies.

feedback.reason: The acknowledgement is the commit boundary between temporary device copies and durable server data.

options.text: Delete local copies only after server acknowledgement.
Keep the local draft objects as the permanent server record and let queue cleanup delete them.
Delete the local draft before server acknowledgement so no duplicate copy exists.
Retain every local draft forever because submitted data must be auditable.

questions.prompt: A canceled offline inspection draft is not retained. Once submitted, a separate server Inspection is durable even if the device later clears its local queue. The same section values are copied during submit rather than transferring the local draft objects. What should happen to local queue objects after a successful submit?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If issue content were intentionally mutable and no rejection history were required, an in-place update could be possible.
details.errorCorrection: Do not collapse correction and delivery retry: one changes content and creates a successor, the other repeats delivery of the same immutable object.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Lifecycle transitions distinguish retrying an operation on the same record from creating a new versioned record.
details.scenarioApplication: Retry keeps the existing identity; correction creates a linked new issue while preserving the rejected one.
details.transfer: Use explicit identity and retention rules to decide whether an operation mutates, retries, or creates a successor.

messages.text: The rejected record is immutable and retained; corrected content has a distinct issue identity.
Delivery retry is not a content correction and the prompt explicitly keeps the same issue ID.
The rejected issue remains part of the audit history after correction.

feedback.reason: Retry repeats an immutable issue, while corrected content has a new identity.

options.text: Retry the same issue ID; create a successor only for corrected content.
Overwrite the rejected issue in place with corrected fields and keep its old ID.
Create a new issue record for every delivery retry, even when its content is unchanged.
Delete the rejected issue after creating the corrected issue.

questions.prompt: A rejected invoice issue is immutable and retained with its rejection reason. A corrected issue gets a new issue ID and links to the rejected one. Retrying delivery of the same issue does not create another issue record. How should retry and correction affect the invoice objects?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the product treated badge records as transient and retained no history, deletion could be allowed, but replacement identity still must not falsely represent the old card.
details.errorCorrection: Do not reuse identity after revocation; the prompt requires the old badge to remain distinguishable.

details.transfer: Model the lifecycle of the physical credential separately from the lifecycle of its person or account.

messages.text: Revocation preserves the old record and replacement gets a new identity.
Every access decision must see the revoked status; caller-local memory does not satisfy that shared state.
A holder account can remain active while one physical badge is revoked.

feedback.reason: Revocation removes access without erasing the retained badge record.

options.text: Revoke and retain the old Badge; give replacement hardware a new ID.
Delete the badge on revocation and reuse its ID for the replacement.
Keep the badge active but ask each door to remember the revocation event separately.
Change the holder’s account status and leave the badge lifecycle unchanged.

questions.prompt: Badge revocation immediately ends access, but the badge record and revocation event are retained. A replacement physical badge receives a new badge ID; the old record is never reactivated. What lifecycle transition represents revocation?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If previews themselves were legally issued documents, they would need the retained artifact lifecycle too.
details.errorCorrection: Do not give the preview the printed artifact’s audit lifetime or delete the artifact with the shipment.

details.scenarioApplication: Cancel removes the preview; successful print creates a distinct durable Label tied to the approved snapshot.
details.transfer: Represent preview, approval, and issued artifact as separate lifecycle stages when their retention differs.

messages.text: Approval and printing define the artifact creation boundary; the preview is not the retained printed record.
The printed label is explicitly retained after shipment cancellation.
Canceled previews are temporary and the prompt does not require them as audit records.

feedback.reason: Preview and printed-label lifetimes begin and end at different workflow events.

options.text: Discard previews on cancel; create a retained Label only after printing.
Promote the preview object into the permanent label before the address is approved.
Delete the printed label when the shipment is canceled, just like the preview.
Keep every abandoned preview permanently as if it had been printed.

questions.prompt: A label preview is temporary and may be discarded when address editing is canceled. A printed label is an immutable audit artifact retained after shipment cancellation. Printing creates a new artifact from the current approved shipment snapshot. Which lifecycle should apply to the preview and printed label?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the product retained expired holds for analytics, it could keep a separate HoldEvent record without turning it into a Booking.

details.scenarioApplication: The Hold exists while awaiting confirmation; expiration removes it, while confirmation creates a durable Booking.
details.transfer: Use explicit confirmation and expiry events to define when a tentative object becomes a durable domain object.

messages.text: An expired unconfirmed hold is not a booking under the stated lifecycle.
The prompt says the Booking exists only after confirmation; early creation exposes the wrong object state.
Expired temporary holds are removed rather than kept as room-owned history.

feedback.reason: Confirmation creates the durable Booking; expiry removes only the ten-minute Hold. Treating the Hold as the Booking would leave a booking after the prompt says none exists.

options.text: Expire the Hold; create a Booking only after confirmation.
Keep an expired Hold as the permanent Booking even when no confirmation arrived.
Create a Booking at hold creation and delete it later if confirmation never arrives.
Let the room record own every Hold forever, including expired unconfirmed holds.

questions.prompt: A rehearsal hold blocks a room for ten minutes while the coordinator waits for confirmation. If confirmation arrives, the system creates a Booking that remains until canceled. If the hold expires, it is removed and no Booking exists. How should hold expiry affect the two objects?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If listings held live PolicyVersion references instead of snapshots, the model would also need to preserve referential integrity for those consumers.
details.errorCorrection: Reference-count retirement is the wrong rule because listings contain copies. Immediate deletion violates retention; indefinite retention ignores the stated purge boundary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Supersession ends availability for new work, while a separate retention clock and hold determine when the version record may be purged.
details.scenarioApplication: The two-year period starts at replacement. Copied listing values do not pin the PolicyVersion, and an active legal hold prevents purge after the period.
details.transfer: Distinguish “not current,” “no longer referenced,” and “eligible for deletion”; a retention schedule can make these separate lifecycle states.

messages.text: The approved two-year retention period applies even though listings copy values and no longer reference the version.
Supersession stops new use, but the required retention period has just begun.
The prompt gives a finite retention period and says listings do not reference the old version.

feedback.reason: A fixed schedule, not remaining listing links, controls purge eligibility here.

options.text: Supersede at replacement; purge after two years unless a legal hold remains.
Purge it as soon as the last listing stops using it, even if two years have not elapsed.
Purge it immediately at replacement because listings have copied its values.
Keep it forever because historical listings must continue to reference the old version.

questions.prompt: When a new catalog policy is published, the prior PolicyVersion stops being available for new listings. Existing listings contain complete copies of the policy values, not references to that PolicyVersion. The approved retention schedule keeps every superseded version for two years after replacement; a legal hold pauses purge. When may the old version be purged?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the product required hard deletion and no completion referred to the revision, reference cleanup could be part of retirement.
details.errorCorrection: Do not treat a newer revision as a replacement for the historical object recorded by a completion.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Retirement changes availability, not historical identity or retention, when records must continue referencing the old version.
details.scenarioApplication: The revision remains resolvable for completion history but is excluded from new enrollment.
details.transfer: Separate an object’s availability to new work from its retention for existing references.

messages.text: The prompt explicitly preserves both revision identity and completion history.
A completion records the exact revision used; retargeting changes its historical meaning.
Retirement is specifically defined to stop new enrollment while preserving existing history.

feedback.reason: Completion history still points to the exact retired revision, so replacing or deleting that identity would break the retained record. Retirement only removes it from future enrollment.

options.text: Retire the revision from enrollment; retain its linked completions.
Delete the revision and cascade-delete its completion records.
Rewrite every completion to point to the newest lesson revision.
Keep the retired revision available for new enrollment because existing completions reference it.

questions.prompt: A lesson revision can be retired from new enrollment while existing completions continue to reference it. A completion record stores the exact revision and remains available for the learner’s history. Retirement must not rewrite or remove completed records. What lifecycle change should retirement perform?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If export intentionally streamed a visible partial archive, the partial artifact would need its own resumable lifecycle contract.
details.errorCorrection: Do not tie the durable archive’s lifetime to the editor session that produced it.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A successful export commits a distinct retained artifact; the live session remains the owner of unsaved working state until that boundary.
details.scenarioApplication: On failure, the session and strokes remain. On success, a separate archive is created and the session may later be deleted.
details.transfer: Preserve the authoritative working object until a durable successor is committed.

messages.text: A failed export must leave the strokes available for retry, so deleting the session first loses required state.
The archive explicitly survives session deletion and therefore has a separate lifetime.
The prompt says no archive is visible until export succeeds; callers should not clean up a partial public object.

feedback.reason: Failed export leaves the source session retryable; only success creates the archive.

options.text: Keep strokes on export failure; create a separate Archive after success.
Delete the Session and its strokes before attempting export.
Treat the Archive as part of the Session so closing the Session deletes the successful export.
Create a partial Archive during export and ask the caller to remove it if export fails.

questions.prompt: A whiteboard session owns unsaved strokes until close. A successful export creates a separate immutable HistoryArchive that survives session deletion. If export fails, no archive is visible and the session keeps its strokes for retry. What should close and export do to these objects?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the system stored only current assignment and no event history, updating a single current record could be sufficient.
details.errorCorrection: Do not use the latest event as mutable storage for current state when the prompt requires an immutable timeline.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Current state and immutable lifecycle events serve different time horizons and should not be collapsed.
details.scenarioApplication: The Conversation reflects the current owner; each reassignment appends a new event while older event values remain intact.
details.transfer: When past facts must remain inspectable, model each transition as a retained event rather than rewriting it.

messages.text: Earlier events must remain a record of their original team/deadline, not be overwritten by current state.
The timeline is explicitly retained after reassignment.
The conversation timeline remains the authoritative event history; team copies are not the stated model.

feedback.reason: Each event captures the team and deadline at its own time, so rewriting an earlier event would erase historical values. Current assignment belongs on the conversation, with a new event recording the transition.

options.text: Change current assignment and append an immutable EscalationEvent.
Rewrite the latest event in place so it always matches the current team and deadline.
Delete old escalation events when ownership changes.
Copy the full history onto each newly assigned team and delete the conversation events.

questions.prompt: A support conversation can change its assigned team several times. Each EscalationEvent records the team and deadline at that time and remains in the timeline. Reassignment updates the current conversation fields but does not mutate older events. How should reassignment affect the escalation history?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If revisions were not immutable and no order pinned them, in-place update could be a different valid model.
details.errorCorrection: A state label such as “current” does not imply the earlier published object can be deleted when references still use it.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Draft and published objects have separate lifecycles, and publication creates an immutable successor rather than mutating the current record.
details.scenarioApplication: Cancel removes the draft only. Publish creates a new revision and retains the old one as superseded.
details.transfer: Use separate working and published identities when consumers may depend on historical versions.

messages.text: The published revision is immutable; draft editing cannot mutate it.
Canceling a draft must not affect the currently published revision.
Prior revisions remain available to orders that selected them; retargeting loses that history.

feedback.reason: Existing orders pin prior published revisions, so publishing a successor cannot replace those objects in place. Cancel discards only the unpublished draft; publication has a separate retained-revision outcome.

options.text: Discard the draft on cancel; publish a retained successor revision.
Mutate the published revision in place whenever a draft is edited.
Delete the currently published revision when a draft is canceled.
Replace the prior revision object at publish and retarget every existing order.

questions.prompt: A listing has an unpublished seasonal draft and a currently published revision. Canceling the draft must leave the published revision untouched. Publishing a validated draft creates a new immutable revision and marks the prior revision superseded; prior revisions remain available to orders that selected them. What lifecycle should draft cancellation and publication use?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If vendors could retract acknowledged work and no record was retained, the accepted-stage retention requirement would differ.
details.errorCorrection: Do not let request cancellation erase a committed vendor obligation, and do not expose one before commitment.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A state transition may create a durable successor with a new lifecycle instead of extending the tentative object in place.
details.scenarioApplication: Before acknowledgement, the tentative split is deleted with the request; after acknowledgement, the separate vendor work order is retained.
details.transfer: Identify the commit event that changes an object from provisional working state to a durable external record.

messages.text: Acknowledgement is the explicit creation boundary for the retained work order.
Accepted vendor work survives later customer cancellation under the stated facts.
The prompt gives the tentative and accepted stages different lifetimes.

feedback.reason: Acknowledgement separates disposable tentative work from retained vendor work.

options.text: Delete tentative splits; retain VendorWorkOrder after acknowledgement.
Create the retained work order before vendor acknowledgement and delete it on request cancellation.
Delete accepted vendor work orders whenever the customer cancels the request.
Treat tentative and accepted splits as one object whose lifetime always matches the request.

questions.prompt: A backorder split is tentative until a vendor acknowledges its portion. Before acknowledgement, canceling the request deletes that tentative split. Return the current wall-clock reading for every call.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This local lifecycle response does not promise network-level exactly-once delivery; distributed retry identity would require a separate stated protocol.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A lifecycle state handles operations appropriate to that stage and preserves terminal outcomes. Repeated requests can return the terminal result without reopening earlier states.
details.scenarioApplication: Confirmed checks in; held can expire; released remains released and is not checked in. The endpoint does not need each client to own these rules.
details.transfer: Keep terminal-state behavior explicit, and do not infer distributed guarantees from a local state machine.

messages.text: The prompt permits check-in from confirmed; a live hold alone is not the required confirmation transition.
A repeated successful check-in must return the existing check-in result, not reject or create a different reservation.
Released cannot be checked in; only a prior successful check-in has an existing check-in result to return.

feedback.reason: The repeated result belongs to the checked-in stage; held and released remain ineligible. The reservation lifecycle can distinguish all three outcomes without claiming network-level exactly-once delivery.

options.text: Let reservation stage govern check-in and return its existing result after a successful repeat.
Allow check-in from held whenever its expiry has not passed, without first confirming the reservation.
Reject every check-in after the first successful one and require clients to create a new reservation to recover the result.
Return the original check-in result for released reservations as well as checked-in reservations.

questions.prompt: A reservation is held, confirmed, checked in, or released. A held reservation may expire; check-in is allowed only after confirmation; release prevents check-in. After a successful check-in, repeating the same request returns its existing check-in result. What should the lifecycle return?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A central API authorization check still matters for access control; it is separate from the case's stage-specific behavior.
details.errorCorrection: Disabling a button is the closest UI-only alternative, but it cannot prevent a stale or automated caller from sending the same request.
details.mechanismOrProperty: State-specific operations keep legal behavior at the lifecycle owner. A resolved state can expose reopen and reject response until a successful transition returns to an active stage.
details.scenarioApplication: Open and awaiting-customer states accept response; resolved requires reopen first. The screen may mirror this rule but does not own it.
details.transfer: Treat presentation affordances as guidance and enforce state-dependent legal operations at the lifecycle owner.

messages.text: Resolved cases require a reopen transition before another response is accepted.
The webhook uses the same case operation and could append a response to a resolved case without reopening it.
The prompt defines reopen as a separate operation; merging it into response hides the required transition from the caller.

feedback.reason: The resolved stage permits reopening but not responding. The case's current state should enforce that distinction even when a request comes from a caller other than the current interface.

options.text: Delegate response and reopen to the active case state so resolved rejects responses and permits reopening before more work.
Accept a response on a resolved case and append it while leaving the case marked resolved.
Hide the response action in the agent screen but accept webhook responses in every stage.
Treat a response to a resolved case as an implicit reopen, then append the response in the same call.

questions.prompt: A support case can be open, awaiting customer, resolved, or reopened. Agents may add a response while open or awaiting customer; resolved cases accept a reopen request, but not another response until reopened. What should the case do with response and reopen calls?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The state machine models the job's local lifecycle; it does not by itself guarantee that an external worker has acknowledged or durably recorded a stop request.
details.errorCorrection: Immediate cancellation is the closest uniform response, but it claims a running worker has stopped before the scenario says that has happened.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Current state owns the operation's permitted result and transition. This distinguishes a request to stop from a completed stop and a terminal success that must remain downloadable.
details.scenarioApplication: Queued is removed, running receives a stop request, and succeeded retains its output. The job service does not report all three as the same canceled state.
details.transfer: Name lifecycle states and outcomes precisely when an operation is a request in one stage and a completed result in another.

messages.text: The running state only requests a cooperative stop; reporting cancellation before the worker stops claims an outcome that has not occurred.
Succeeded jobs must remain available for download; the output and status would contradict each other.
A queued job has not begun running; the prompt says cancellation removes it rather than waiting for a nonexistent running worker.

feedback.reason: A cancel request means different things in queued, running, and succeeded states. The job lifecycle should choose the correct transition or preservation outcome instead of treating the endpoint name as one universal action.

options.text: Have the job's current state implement cancellation: queued removes, running requests stop, and succeeded preserves the downloadable result.
Mark a running job canceled as soon as the request arrives, even though its worker has not stopped.
Delete a succeeded job's output when cancel is retried, then leave its success status for download clients.
Send a stop request for a queued job and keep it queued until a worker eventually acknowledges it.

questions.prompt: A batch job is queued, running, succeeded, or failed. Canceling a queued job removes it; canceling a running job requests cooperative stop; succeeded jobs remain available for download. The same cancel call is used in all stages. Which design keeps these outcomes consistent?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If only the view should hide controls, that is a presentation rule. The document still needs to reject an illegal mutation when invoked directly.
details.errorCorrection: A boolean can look sufficient, but it does not encode the submitted stage that is required before signing and can create invalid combinations with an edit flag.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A single current state represents the lifecycle stage. Each state's operation handlers permit only the transitions supported there, including a signed state with no mutation transition.
details.scenarioApplication: Editable accepts edits, submitted accepts signing, and signed preserves its content. No screen-specific status copy is needed for correctness.
details.transfer: Represent ordered, mutually exclusive lifecycle stages explicitly when several operations depend on them and a terminal stage forbids mutation.

messages.text: The contract says a signed document cannot be edited; an audit note does not restore the original signed content.
A caller can bypass the screen and alter a submitted or signed document despite the lifecycle rule.
The prompt defines three ordered stages, so independent flags can allow contradictory combinations and skip the submission transition.

feedback.reason: Edit and sign legality both depend on a mutually exclusive document stage, and signature is terminal. The document lifecycle owner should decide operations and transitions rather than trusting each editor screen.

options.text: Let editable, submitted, and signed states decide edit and sign; the signed state rejects both edits and any unsigned transition.
Allow edits after signature and store an audit note that the document changed later.
Have each editor screen block changes after submission and let the document accept direct edits.
Use a single signed boolean and permit a document to be both editable and submitted until that flag is set.

questions.prompt: A document moves from editable to submitted to signed. Editing is allowed only before submission; signing is allowed only after submission; a signed document cannot be edited or unsigned. Which owner should decide the result of edit and sign requests?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Returning an existing result is a scenario-level local retry contract; it does not imply exactly-once processing across remote gateway failures.
details.errorCorrection: Client-side status handling is the closest alternative, but a stale display can repeat capture or let a decline reach a prohibited transition.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Each state owns behavior for capture. Approved can make the transition; captured can provide its existing outcome; pending and declined reject it.
details.scenarioApplication: The caller uses one capture operation, while the current authorization state preserves the distinction among pending, approved, declined, and captured.
details.transfer: Model repeat behavior and terminal outcomes explicitly without claiming stronger distributed guarantees than the stated lifecycle provides.

messages.text: Capture is legal only after approval; a later void does not make the premature capture valid.
After capture, a retry must return the existing capture result rather than create another capture.
Declined is terminal for capture in this lifecycle; a retry cannot convert that result to approval.

feedback.reason: The payment lifecycle determines eligibility and the retry result. The authorization should enforce the allowed transitions and return its captured result rather than delegating the state table to clients.

options.text: Allow capture only from approved; a captured retry returns its stored result.
Allow capture while pending and void the capture later if the authorization is declined.
Submit a new capture on every retry and reconcile any duplicate charges during reporting.
Treat a declined authorization as approved when a client repeats capture with the same request.

questions.prompt: A payment authorization is pending, approved, declined, or captured. Capture is legal only after approval, and capture retry after capture must return the existing capture result. A decline cannot transition to captured. How should the authorization answer these calls?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An external rental inventory may need a separate capacity protocol; this scenario only specifies the contract's local lifecycle behavior.
details.errorCorrection: Requiring overdue to reset is a plausible simplification, but it inserts a transition the prompt does not define and blocks an allowed return.
details.mechanismOrProperty: State-specific handlers allow an operation from more than one state when the contract says so, and terminal state can return the prior outcome without repeating the transition.
details.scenarioApplication: Checked-out and overdue transition to returned; returned supplies the receipt on retry. Only available can check out again.
details.transfer: A state machine need not be a simple linear sequence: let each state expose the operations and repeated outcomes the contract actually permits.

messages.text: Return is explicitly allowed from overdue; an extra transition blocks a valid return.
A repeat must return the existing receipt, not create a second one.
Check-out is permitted only from available, and overdue remains an active rental stage.

feedback.reason: Availability governs check-out, while both active-rental stages can return and the returned stage has a stable repeat result. The contract state can apply those distinctions at the lifecycle owner.

options.text: Check out only when available; return from checked-out or overdue, then replay the returned receipt.
Require an overdue contract to become checked out again before it can be returned.
Create a new return receipt each time a returned contract receives the same return request.
Allow a new check-out from overdue while the original rental is still active.

questions.prompt: A rental contract is available, checked out, overdue, or returned. Check-out is permitted only when available; return is permitted from checked out or overdue; returning twice returns the existing return receipt. How should the contract handle these operations?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: State does not replace authorization: the service must still identify whether the caller has the role to perform an allowed stage operation.
details.errorCorrection: Role screens are a useful affordance, but the stated shared API means another caller could bypass their stage checks.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Current state controls legal operations and transitions. The state can record whether the single appeal transition has occurred without making unrelated callers own the lifecycle matrix.
details.scenarioApplication: Under review accepts evidence; upheld permits one appeal; dismissed has no reopen transition. Screens may expose allowed actions but cannot be the only enforcement point.
details.transfer: Separate who may act from which lifecycle operations are legal; let the state govern the latter at the entity that owns it.

messages.text: Dismissed items cannot be reopened, so accepting an appeal there violates the terminal-stage rule.
The prompt allows an appeal once; additional evidence does not make a second appeal legal.
The shared item API would still allow operations that the lifecycle excludes, regardless of what a screen displays.

feedback.reason: Evidence, appeal, and reopening have different permissions at different stages. The item lifecycle should enforce them consistently, while role authorization remains a separate concern.

options.text: Permit evidence during review, one appeal after uphold, and no reopening after dismissal.
Permit appeals from both upheld and dismissed stages, then let staff decide whether dismissal is reversible.
Allow an upheld item to accept unlimited appeals as long as each has new evidence.
Hide appeal and evidence actions in the screens but let the item API accept them in any stage.

questions.prompt: A moderation item is new, under review, upheld, or dismissed. Reviewers may add evidence while under review; upheld items can be appealed once; dismissed items cannot be reopened. The same item API serves reviewers and appeal staff. What should govern those calls?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This state model does not decide worker concurrency or durable job recovery; those would need separate scenario requirements.
details.errorCorrection: Scheduler-only validation looks centralized, but it cannot enforce the lifecycle for the other API callers the prompt names.
details.mechanismOrProperty: State-specific behavior can allow operations at a particular stage and forbid mutation after terminal success. This keeps the transition rules with the object whose lifecycle advances.
details.scenarioApplication: Unconfigured accepts configuration, ready can execute, failed can retry, and succeeded rejects mutation; the scheduler is not the sole correctness boundary.
details.transfer: Enforce stage-dependent transitions at the shared lifecycle owner when several entry points invoke its operations.

messages.text: Diagnostic and retry tools also invoke the API, so scheduler-only checks do not protect the shared build lifecycle.
Configuration is only legal before execution; changing inputs mid-run violates that stage boundary.
Retry is permitted only after failure; an unconfigured build has not reached that state.

feedback.reason: The build API has multiple callers, but legal operations depend on the build stage. Enforcing the transition on the build keeps scheduler, diagnostic, and retry paths consistent.

options.text: Have the build's current state enforce configure-before-run, retry-after-failure, and no mutation after success.
Let the scheduler enforce all stages and allow other build API clients to call configure or retry directly.
Allow configure during execution and replace the build inputs used by the running worker.
Let retry restart any unsuccessful build, including one that has never been configured.

questions.prompt: A build is unconfigured, ready, executing, succeeded, or failed. Configure is allowed only before execution; retry is allowed only after failure; succeeded builds are immutable. A scheduler invokes operations through one build API. Where do these rules belong?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The exception request does not promise that a carrier changes the destination; the scenario only establishes that a separate request is required.
details.errorCorrection: The screen could branch on carrier status, but scanner and support tools also call the parcel API and could make a stale local rewrite.
details.mechanismOrProperty: State-specific operations distinguish a local mutation before handoff from an exception request after handoff. Terminal state rejects a transition that would contradict completed delivery.
details.scenarioApplication: Before acceptance the label can change; after acceptance the separate exception path is used; delivered remains delivered.
details.transfer: Represent an external handoff as a lifecycle boundary when it changes which operations may mutate local state.

messages.text: After acceptance, the local label must not be rewritten; correction uses a separate exception request.
Delivery is terminal; changing an address cannot reverse that completed lifecycle state.
The prompt allows correction only before acceptance; a later edit cannot substitute for the required exception request.

feedback.reason: Carrier acceptance changes which correction is legal, and delivery is terminal. The parcel state can preserve the handoff boundary instead of allowing every caller to rewrite the same address.

options.text: Edit before acceptance; afterward issue an exception, and keep delivery terminal.
Rewrite the accepted carrier label after handoff and send a correction notice as a separate step.
Let support return a delivered parcel to in-transit when it changes the address.
Allow an address correction in transit by editing the label and notifying the carrier afterward.

questions.prompt: A parcel is labeled, accepted by a carrier, in transit, or delivered. Address corrections are allowed before carrier acceptance; after acceptance, correction must create a separate exception request rather than rewrite the label. Delivery is terminal. How should the parcel handle correction and delivery calls?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Seat allocation itself may be a separate service; this question asks how enrollment applies the resulting stage and prerequisite.
details.errorCorrection: Searching for a seat after confirming is the nearest alternative, but the prompt requires assignment before confirmation.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The enrollment's current state governs transitions, including prerequisites that must be satisfied before a state change. The caller does not reconstruct the entire lifecycle table.
details.scenarioApplication: Requested needs a seat, waitlisted accepts an offer, and withdrawn rejects confirmation; both entry points call the same enrollment behavior.
details.transfer: Keep a lifecycle transition from becoming valid before its required prerequisite is satisfied.

messages.text: A seat must be assigned before confirmation; the later search cannot satisfy that prerequisite.
Withdrawn cannot be confirmed or restored by retry; it is the terminal state in the prompt.
A waitlisted learner must accept the offered seat before the enrollment can become confirmed.

feedback.reason: Enrollment operations depend on a mutually exclusive stage and the seat condition. A state-specific owner applies the same rules for registration and support.

options.text: Confirm only with a seat; handle offers separately and reject withdrawn enrollment.
Confirm a waitlisted learner first and search for a seat afterward if one becomes free.
Reopen a withdrawn enrollment when registration retries confirmation, then treat it as requested.
Confirm after a waitlist offer is sent, even if the learner has not accepted it.

questions.prompt: A course enrollment is requested, confirmed, waitlisted, or withdrawn. Confirmation is allowed only after a seat is assigned; a waitlisted learner may accept an offered seat; a withdrawn enrollment cannot be confirmed. The same enrollment methods are used by registration and support. What should decide each result?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This local return lifecycle does not guarantee remote payment settlement or exactly-once provider behavior.
details.errorCorrection: Client checks are attractive because each caller knows its action, but independent checks can diverge and do not centralize the shared refund retry behavior.
details.mechanismOrProperty: State-specific behavior applies operation prerequisites at the lifecycle owner and can return the existing outcome from a terminal state.
details.scenarioApplication: Authorized permits receipt; received permits refund; refunded returns the stored record. The warehouse and finance clients do not own separate status matrices.
details.transfer: Place stage prerequisites and terminal repeat outcomes with the lifecycle whose state they govern.

messages.text: Refund is permitted only after receipt, so this performs the financial operation before its stated prerequisite.
A return must be authorized before receipt; a scan is not the required authorization transition.
The refunded state must return the existing refund record, not create a duplicate.

feedback.reason: The return has ordered stages, and each operation is legal only after its prerequisite. Keeping that transition logic on the return gives warehouse and finance callers one consistent result.

options.text: Receive only after authorization; refund after receipt, then replay the stored result.
Refund when the return is requested and let the warehouse record receipt afterward.
Receive an item directly from requested and infer authorization from the warehouse scan.
Create another refund record whenever a caller repeats the request after the first refund.

questions.prompt: A package return is requested, authorized, received, or refunded. A warehouse can receive only an authorized return; refund is permitted only after receipt; duplicate refund requests return the existing refund record. Which component should own those rules?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The prompt assumes the booking can determine hold validity when handling confirmation; it makes no claim about synchronized clocks or distributed expiry guarantees.
details.errorCorrection: Cleanup-after-confirmation is the tempting alternative, but it exposes a confirmed state that the hold prerequisite forbids.
details.mechanismOrProperty: State-specific operations can check transition prerequisites and preserve terminal outcomes. The state owner centralizes the result for callers without making cancellation reversible.
details.scenarioApplication: A valid hold can confirm; an expired hold cannot; a canceled booking stays canceled and returns the original cancellation result.
details.transfer: Evaluate a transition's stated prerequisite at the lifecycle operation that performs the transition, not as later cleanup.

messages.text: An expired hold is not eligible for confirmation; later cleanup exposes an invalid confirmed booking.
Canceled is terminal, and repetition must return its existing cancellation result.
The prompt requires the same cancellation result on repetition, not an error.

feedback.reason: The live-hold prerequisite changes whether confirmation is legal, while canceled has a terminal repeat result. The booking's state should enforce both behaviors.

options.text: Confirm only a valid hold; canceled stays terminal and repeats its result.
Confirm a held booking after its deadline and let a cleanup job cancel it later.
Reopen a canceled booking as tentative when a cancellation request is repeated.
Reject every repeated cancel request after the first cancellation, even when the caller asks for the same result.

questions.prompt: A booking is tentative, held, confirmed, or canceled. A held booking may be confirmed only while its hold remains valid; a canceled booking cannot be restored, and a repeated cancellation returns the original cancellation result. How should the booking respond?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The command representation does not itself make review durable or transactional; those guarantees must come from the surrounding storage and approval contract.
details.errorCorrection: Reading components later from the live catalog is the closest lightweight alternative, but it changes the object under review if the catalog changes meanwhile.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A command packages an operation and its arguments as an identifiable value. The receiver can validate or defer that value before it changes the catalog.
details.scenarioApplication: The proposal carries components and policy version together; rejection changes nothing, while acceptance applies the validated bundle change.
details.transfer: Use an operation value when a review or delayed decision must remain tied to the exact inputs originally proposed.

messages.text: The prompt requires a rejected proposal to leave the catalog unchanged and a stable component set for review; mutating live data exposes an unapproved intermediate value.
That loses the exact proposed components and policy version the reviewer is meant to assess.
Independent screens can use different component or policy versions, so the submitted price may not match the proposal under review.

feedback.reason: The review concerns one proposed operation, not a mutable live bundle. Capturing its inputs lets the system validate that exact change and apply it only after approval.

options.text: Capture components and policy version in a reviewable command; validate before applying.
Mutate the live bundle while reviewers are still choosing components, then roll it back if they reject it.
Store only the bundle ID and read whatever component set is current when a reviewer eventually opens it.
Ask each review screen to calculate the bundle price independently and submit its own total.

questions.prompt: A catalog manager adds a regional bundle whose price must equal the sum of its current components. The requested component set and policy version must be captured for review; a rejected bundle leaves the catalog unchanged. Which representation gives the proposed operation a stable reviewable identity?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The scenario specifies a local retry identity contract; it does not establish durable exactly-once behavior across process or storage failures.
details.errorCorrection: Equal-value matching is the tempting alternative, but two independent requests can ask for the same charger and expiry and still represent separate intents.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An operation object can carry a request identifier and the inputs needed to execute it. Deduplication is keyed to that stated identity, not merely equal business values.
details.scenarioApplication: The station evaluates capacity and expiry for the identified request, then a retry using that identity receives the associated reservation result.
details.transfer: Distinguish repeated delivery of one operation from a new operation by carrying explicit intent identity when retries are possible.

messages.text: The same values could be an intentional second reservation; without identity, the receiver cannot know this is the original attempt.
That consumes a second capacity slot for the same requested reservation, contrary to the retry contract.
A distinct identified request may be a separate reservation; matching the charger alone conflates separate intents.

feedback.reason: The client may not know whether its first request succeeded. A stable command identity lets the receiver recognize the same intent and return its original reservation outcome rather than consume capacity again.

options.text: Give the reservation command a stable request identity and return the result already associated with that identity on retry.
Retry by sending the same charger and expiry values as a fresh reservation with no request identity.
Decrement capacity when the first request is sent and decrement it again when the client retries.
Treat any later request for the same charger as a duplicate, even when it has a different request identity.

questions.prompt: A station operator reserves a charger only if capacity remains and the requested expiry fits the station's limit. A client may retry the same reservation request after losing its response; the retry must return the original reservation rather than consume capacity again. What should identify the request?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This local reversible edit does not imply a general audit-retention or multi-user conflict policy beyond the prompt.
details.errorCorrection: A whole-object replacement is the nearest alternative, but it would replace identity along with descriptive data, contrary to the preservation fact.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A command can retain target identity and the values needed for execution and reversal. The receiver applies those values to the existing asset rather than replacing its identity.
details.scenarioApplication: Approval writes the proposed metadata; undo restores the captured prior metadata on the same asset ID.
details.transfer: For reversible edits, preserve the operation's target identity and the exact prior values needed to reverse its effect.

messages.text: The prompt requires the asset identity to remain stable; replacing the asset violates that condition even if its values look restored.
That loses the prior descriptive values required for a reliable approved undo.
Without a captured change, the system cannot tell which prior values belong to this reviewed merge.

feedback.reason: The merge must be reviewable and reversible, but the asset itself is not being replaced. Recording the exact before-and-after values gives the operation enough information to apply or undo its own change.

options.text: Record asset ID and before/after values so approved undo restores the same asset.
Replace the asset with a new object on undo and assign it a new identity containing the old metadata.
Keep only the latest metadata values and ask an archivist to reconstruct the prior values if undo is requested.
Allow the review screen to edit the asset directly and infer undo by reversing whatever fields changed last.

questions.prompt: An archivist merges duplicate metadata while the asset's identity remains stable. The edit must be reviewable before commit, and an approved undo must restore the prior descriptive values without replacing the asset itself. Which representation supports that history?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The command carries intent; the scenario does not promise that an external licensing registry remains current or that queue delivery is durable.
details.errorCorrection: Checking only at enqueue is plausible for immediate work, but the prompt says the request can wait and requires authorization at execution.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A command object carries operation arguments through a queue and can be inspected before execution. The receiver still performs the stated authorization check when it acts.
details.scenarioApplication: Territory and expiry travel with the queued approval; the executing analyst is checked and recorded when that exact scope is granted.
details.transfer: Queued operations should carry the arguments that define their intent, while execution-time rules are evaluated at the point specified by the contract.

messages.text: The worker would not have the scope that the analyst requested, so the eventual approval could authorize different use.
The prompt assigns the check to execution; an enqueue-time decision may no longer reflect the executing analyst's authority.
That changes both the requested scope and expiration before execution, then records attribution too late to constrain the approval.

feedback.reason: The queued operation must preserve the analyst's requested scope until execution, where the scenario requires authorization. Capturing its fields and recording the actor makes the executed approval attributable to the actual decision.

options.text: Queue territory and expiry; recheck authority at execution and record the actor and approved scope.
Queue only the analyst's name and ask the worker to infer the territory and expiry from current defaults.
Check authority when the request is enqueued and never recheck when the delayed command executes.
Let the worker grant the default territory indefinitely and add the analyst attribution afterward.

questions.prompt: A licensing analyst approves use in one territory until a stated expiration. The approval can wait in a review queue; authorization must be checked when it is executed, and the record must retain the analyst, territory, and expiry used. What should the queue hold?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This scenario explicitly supplies the compare-before-undo condition; it does not imply a general concurrency-control implementation.
details.errorCorrection: Unconditional clearing is the tempting inverse, but it can overwrite a later assignment that the original operation did not create.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A command stores the target and the before-and-after values it changes. Conditional undo compares current state with the command's expected result before applying its inverse.
details.scenarioApplication: The record carries the battery and both aircraft IDs; undo restores the prior relationship only if the replacement relationship is still present.
details.transfer: An inverse operation should verify that the state it plans to reverse is still the state produced by the original command.

messages.text: That can erase a later valid assignment; the prompt permits undo only while the recorded replacement association still holds.
The current roster may have changed, so it cannot supply the prior association captured when this operation was approved.
A battery cannot belong to two aircraft, and a duplicate record does not reverse the original assignment.

feedback.reason: A replacement can be reversed only while its own resulting assignment remains current. Capturing both ends makes that precondition check possible and avoids clearing a later reassignment.

options.text: Record the battery and both aircraft IDs; undo only if its replacement assignment still matches.
Undo by clearing the battery's current aircraft assignment regardless of who assigned it afterward.
Store only the replacement aircraft and infer the prior aircraft from the current fleet roster at undo time.
Undo by creating a second battery record for the former aircraft and leaving the original assignment in place.

questions.prompt: A fleet coordinator schedules a battery replacement. Each battery may belong to only one aircraft, and an approved replacement can be undone only if that battery is still assigned to the aircraft recorded by the operation. What must the replacement record contain?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The scenario specifies this consent check and recipient binding; it does not promise transactional coordination with an external specialist system.
details.errorCorrection: Resolving the recipient later is convenient, but it changes the approved destination and therefore changes the action the patient consented to.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A command carries the arguments that define an operation across delay. The receiver evaluates current execution-time conditions before performing the requested effect.
details.scenarioApplication: The command uses the approved specialist and makes no disclosure if consent has been withdrawn by execution time.
details.transfer: For delayed sensitive actions, preserve the approved target and re-evaluate any stated revocable prerequisite before execution.

messages.text: The recipient could change after approval, so the worker may disclose to a specialist the patient did not approve.
The prompt requires execution to check current consent and prohibits disclosure after withdrawal.
That makes the recipient choice independent of the one approved by the patient and checks consent only after disclosure.

feedback.reason: The pending route has a fixed approved recipient but a revocable prerequisite. Capturing the recipient and checking consent when the action executes preserves both parts of that intent.

options.text: Queue the approved recipient; recheck consent at execution before disclosure.
Queue a referral ID and resolve whichever specialist is currently assigned when the worker executes it.
Send the referral immediately when consent is granted and ignore a withdrawal that occurs before the queued work completes.
Let each routing worker choose a recipient and record consent status after sending.

questions.prompt: A care navigator routes a referral only after the patient consents to external disclosure. The routing request can be prepared in advance, but execution must use the exact recipient approved by the patient; if consent is withdrawn before execution, no disclosure occurs. What should represent the pending action?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The prompt assumes those referenced versions remain available; it does not specify a long-term retention or archive policy.
details.errorCorrection: Looking up the latest version is the common shortcut, but it changes the evaluation after the learner has already performed the attempt.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A command packages a deferred operation with the values that determine its meaning. Recording version identifiers makes the requested evaluation independent of later defaults.
details.scenarioApplication: The attempt starts with a specific exercise and policy revision; completion carries those IDs to the grader and uses them after the instructor publishes a new version.
details.transfer: When deferred work must preserve the conditions under which it began, capture the relevant version identities with the operation.

messages.text: The current values may have changed after the attempt began and would grade work under rules the learner did not use.
That omits the exact revision and policy the attempt must retain, so the later grader cannot reliably select them.
That changes the rules of an attempt already underway, contradicting the requirement to use its start-time versions.

feedback.reason: The grading work may finish after the exercise changes. The completion operation must carry the versions that defined the attempt so later execution cannot silently switch its scoring contract.

options.text: Bind grading to the attempt’s exercise and scoring-policy versions.
Resolve the current exercise and scoring policy when the grading callback runs.
Store only the learner and exercise ID, then ask the instructor to reconstruct which revision was active.
Copy the new revision into every in-progress attempt as soon as it is published.

questions.prompt: A learner completes a timed exercise. The completion record must use the exercise revision and scoring policy visible when the attempt began, even if the instructor publishes a new revision before grading finishes. How should completion carry its intent?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The command records and executes intent; it does not establish how controls are implemented or guarantee a durable queue.
details.errorCorrection: Approving at enqueue is the closest shortcut, but it reverses the required ordering between controls and approval.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A command makes the requested action and its parameters explicit, allowing a worker to execute the same intent later and report its acceptance or rejection.
details.scenarioApplication: The manager, rationale, and scope travel together; required controls run first and any rejection keeps the request pending.
details.transfer: For queued approvals, preserve the actor's scoped request and do not report success before required validation completes.

messages.text: That creates an approved state before the required controls finish and turns a rejection into cleanup rather than a blocked approval.
The queued operation would no longer express the manager's actual rationale or requested scope.

questions.prompt: A licensing analyst approves a usage for one territory and expiry. Catalog, rights evaluation, usage reporting, and notification modules each own separate responsibilities; an approval must reach all of them, but none may infer or change the approved scope. What should route it?

questions.prompt: A procurement exception requires manager attribution, rationale, and approval by both compliance and budget controls.
