constraints: classification and refund eligibility are not the same responsibility
Seal and recall criteria are maintained separately; recall takes precedence when it applies, while refund eligibility remains independent.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separate ordered evaluation is useful while independent review rules can qualify from item facts and precedence matters. If a single authoritative code directly identifies one reviewer, direct dispatch is simpler.
details.errorCorrection: The closest wrong approach is let the caller select a reviewer from the return category before either reviewer checks the seal or recall facts. The category alone does not establish which reviewer can decide this item; choosing before eligibility bypasses the stated ordered checks. The contract instead requires one classification.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An applicable handler returns its result and ends evaluation; a handler whose stated qualification does not apply passes so the next ordered handler can inspect the request. This separates sequencing from each handler’s case-specific eligibility rule.
details.scenarioApplication: The returns workflow needs one classification result that honors recall precedence while leaving refunds to their own decision.
details.transfer: For another return category, keep recall precedence in the classification result and do not absorb refund eligibility into it.

messages.text: The category alone does not establish which reviewer can decide this item; choosing before eligibility bypasses the stated ordered checks.

feedback.reason: Seal evidence determines the ordinary result, but a safety recall takes precedence and refund eligibility remains separate. The design must realize this outcome while leaving rule-specific behavior independently maintained.

options.text: Run classification handlers in order; each returns a class or passes, while refund eligibility stays separate.
Let the caller select a reviewer from the return category before either reviewer checks the seal or recall facts.

Add seal, recall, and future return-class branches to the warehouse dispatcher.
Run both reviews at once and use whichever classification arrives first.

questions.prompt: In a returns inspection workflow, the warehouse inspector must classify a returned item. Refund eligibility is a separate decision, and assessment rules are maintained by separate reviewers. Which design keeps the classification outcome consistent as new assessment rules are added?

constraints: published outputs reference immutable inputs and code versions

details.mechanismOrProperty: An applicable handler returns its result and ends evaluation; a handler whose stated qualification does not apply passes so the next ordered handler can inspect the request. This separates sequencing from each handler’s case-specific eligibility rule.
details.scenarioApplication: A backend is usable only for the requested immutable pair, and configuration provides the winner when several backends are compatible.
details.transfer: For another snapshot pair, preserve exact version matching and use the configured backend preference among compatible choices.

messages.text: Experiment type does not prove backend support for this exact immutable pair; a preselected backend can reject when another ordered backend supports it.

Fast response is not the stated support or ordering criterion and can publish from a later backend.

feedback.reason: Publication must use the exact input/code pair and prefer the highest-ranked compatible backend. The design must realize this outcome while leaving rule-specific behavior independently maintained.

options.text: Choose one snapshot backend from the experiment type before checking support for its input and code version.
Combine snapshot fragments from every backend that supports either the input or the code version.

When more than one backend supports the pair, notebook configuration ranks them and the highest-ranked compatible backend is preferred. Which design preserves that preference without changing publication code for each backend?

questions.prompt: In a procurement approval queue, a manager may approve a bounded exception only after required controls pass. The approval must record who approved it and its scope. A search index and requester notice may update later, and event handling may be retried. Which design fits?

A participant notification is sent after reservation; notification failure may retry by reservation ID and must not create another window. What should coordinate the operation?

constraints: The previous provider remains active if the staged candidate fails its test.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Compensate reversible staging on failure; keep the last known-good provider until validation succeeds.
details.errorCorrection: Switching before validation exposes the live stream to a provider that may violate timing or error behavior.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The coordinator stages a candidate, validates it, and makes one activation decision. Failure discards the candidate and preserves the current provider.
details.scenarioApplication: Only a tested provider receives traffic, and a dashboard delay cannot undo an accepted switch.
details.transfer: For another provider change, test before activation and retain the active implementation if the candidate fails.

messages.text: The candidate must pass the timing/error test before it receives traffic; monitoring is not a substitute for that test.
The old provider must remain active if the staged candidate fails.
A failed configuration is discarded and must not serve traffic under a staged label.
Monitoring may catch up after success; its delay does not undo the accepted provider switch.

feedback.reason: Testing is the acceptance boundary for traffic; the existing provider remains the fallback until the candidate passes.

options.text: Switch only after the candidate passes; retain the active provider on failure.
Move traffic to the candidate first and use monitoring to discover whether timing and errors meet the contract.
Remove the active provider before testing the replacement so the studio cannot use two configurations.
Keep a failed candidate active but label it staged until a later test succeeds.
Restore the old provider whenever the monitoring dashboard is delayed after a passing switch.

questions.prompt: In a live captioning studio, a new provider is configured and tested against timing/error requirements before traffic is switched. If the test fails, the old provider remains active and the staged configuration is discarded. After a successful switch, monitoring may catch up later. Which workflow fits?

constraints: A failed check on either volunteer leaves the original roster unchanged.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Use compensation for temporary locks/holds; persist the paired state only after both conditions succeed.
details.errorCorrection: Committing the first move before checking the second exposes a partial state the prompt forbids.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The coordinator acquires reversible holds, checks both sides, and either commits the pair or compensates all holds.
details.scenarioApplication: No half-swap is visible, and a failed check restores both assignments to the original roster.
details.transfer: For another multi-party change, make the complete participant set explicit and release temporary claims on any failed precondition.

messages.text: The roster would expose a partial swap before both skill and availability checks pass.
The prompt preserves the original roster if either check fails; it does not accept a partially committed pair.
Both temporary holds must be released on either failure, not leave one assignment unavailable.
The audit consumer is not the roster decision owner, and publication cannot turn one move into the required paired swap.

feedback.reason: The roster accepts one paired change, not intermediate assignments that can leave the volunteers in a half-swap.

options.text: Commit the swap only after both checks pass; release both holds on failure.
Move the first volunteer immediately and ask the second volunteer to accept the remaining assignment later.
Commit each assignment as soon as its volunteer passes, then reconcile a failed second check manually.
Retain the first assignment hold when the second volunteer fails so the swap can resume without reacquiring it.
Publish the first move and let the audit consumer complete the second assignment after it records the event.

questions.prompt: In a volunteer coordination hub, a two-person assignment swap requires both volunteers to pass skill and availability checks. Temporary holds are placed on both assignments; if either check fails, release both holds and keep the original roster unchanged. Which workflow preserves the swap?

constraints: The route revision includes geometry, conflict markers, and provenance as one accepted change.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Use the storage transaction for the stated all-record invariant; retry the projection from committed state.
details.errorCorrection: Publishing geometry without its markers/provenance can silently overwrite conflicts, while undoing for a search outage reverses an accepted change unnecessarily.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The workflow has one atomic acceptance boundary for the route records, then treats search as a post-commit projection. No partial route state is published.
details.scenarioApplication: A storage failure leaves the old route authoritative; a search failure after commit does not roll back accepted geometry.
details.transfer: For another offline merge, commit all conflict/provenance data with the route revision and rebuild search afterward.

messages.text: Search is a derived projection; it cannot decide canonical geometry or conflicts.
The route revision is accepted only with all three parts, so geometry alone is not a valid commit.
A search outage occurs after acceptance and must not reverse the stored route revision.
Independent projections could disagree; the prompt requires one accepted revision with the conflict data and provenance.

feedback.reason: Storage decides whether the complete route revision is accepted; search can be regenerated from it afterward.

options.text: Commit geometry, markers, and provenance together; retry search from that accepted revision.
Publish the geometry to search first and let the index choose which merge becomes canonical.
Commit geometry now and attach conflict markers and provenance after storage becomes available.
Undo the full route revision whenever search is unavailable after a successful storage commit.
Let each projection merge its own geometry and resolve conflicts independently.

questions.prompt: In a local-first map editor, a merge is accepted only when geometry, conflict markers, and provenance are stored together. Search is a derived projection and may retry. If storage rejects the merge, no new geometry is accepted; a search outage after commit must not undo it.

constraints: Before ledger commit, failed reward validation restores the temporary item reservation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Compensate only the pre-commit reservation; once the paired ledger transition is committed, repair projections rather than reversing gameplay state.
details.errorCorrection: Treating a projection as the authority for campaign legality can duplicate or invalidate the reward after the owner has committed it.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The workflow compensates a reversible item hold when validation fails, commits the paired ledger change once, and retries summaries from its stable reward identity.
details.scenarioApplication: The campaign has neither a spent item without a reward nor a reward without item consumption; summary lag leaves the accepted ledger unchanged.
details.transfer: For another resource-backed reward, define the pre-commit reservation and rollback separately from post-commit summary work.

messages.text: The prompt requires restoring the item when reward validation fails after reservation.
Item use and the reward must be one accepted ledger change, not separate downstream writes.
Summary refresh is retryable after commit and cannot change the accepted reward ledger entry.
The campaign ledger records the accepted item/reward change; summaries do not own that gameplay decision.

feedback.reason: The ledger accepts item consumption and reward together; summary lag is downstream and cannot rewrite that accepted pair.

options.text: Commit item use with its reward; restore only a failed pre-commit hold and retry summaries.
Consume the item before validating the reward and leave it spent if validation rejects the reward.
Commit item consumption first, then let each achievement summary create the reward entry later.
Undo the committed reward whenever an achievement summary refresh is delayed.
Let an achievement projection decide whether the campaign ledger may consume the item.

questions.prompt: In a board-game campaign manager, consuming a rare item and granting its reward must be one accepted ledger change. If reward validation fails after the item is reserved, restore the item; once the reward ledger entry commits, achievement summaries may retry without changing the ledger.

constraints: Failed temperature eligibility keeps the shipment with its current carrier.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Compensate the temporary reservation, not the previous accepted carrier assignment; treat tracking as a retryable projection.
details.errorCorrection: Changing ownership before temperature validation can place the shipment with an ineligible carrier.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The coordinator holds the candidate resource, validates the shipment constraint, and commits one hand-off only on success. It compensates the hold on failure.
details.scenarioApplication: The shipment remains with its old carrier after a failed check, while an accepted revision gives tracking a stable source for retry.
details.transfer: For another carrier change, validate constraints before transfer and release candidate reservations when the check fails.

messages.text: The shipment would be owned by a carrier that may fail the explicit temperature condition.
The failure outcome releases the candidate reservation while the old carrier keeps the shipment.
Tracking follows an accepted shipment revision; it does not determine carrier eligibility.
Tracking may retry from the accepted shipment revision, so projection lag does not reverse the transfer.

feedback.reason: The shipment remains with its current carrier until eligibility is known; accepted tracking is a later projection.

options.text: Hand off only after temperature passes; release the candidate hold on failure.
Transfer the shipment to the new carrier before temperature validation and repair the assignment if the test fails.
Keep the candidate carrier reserved after a failed temperature test so another attempt can reuse it.
Let tracking accept the hand-off and decide whether the receiving carrier meets the temperature limit.
Undo a valid hand-off whenever the tracking projection has not refreshed yet.

questions.prompt: In a cold-chain logistics console, a receiving carrier is reserved before temperature eligibility is confirmed. If the temperature test fails, the old carrier keeps the shipment and the new carrier reservation is released. After hand-off is accepted, tracking can retry from the shipment revision.

constraints: An export is for one session and must read its committed event sequence.
The storage key and paging scheme may change independently of the board use case.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The repository boundary earns its cost here because multiple domain queries and storage-specific paging must coexist; a small one-table CRUD path would not automatically need a custom repository.
details.errorCorrection: An ORM query in the export handler would couple a domain use case to the current row keys and paging scheme. A cached snapshot adds a freshness contract the prompt never asks for.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Expose sessions and their committed history through a collection-shaped contract; its adapter can page event rows without teaching the export handler their keys.
details.scenarioApplication: For this board, the export requests one session’s committed sequence, while workspace listing is a separate domain query; neither should expose the event table layout.
details.transfer: Use this boundary when callers need domain objects or queries and mapping details vary; keep presentation-only reads as projections when they do not change domain state.

messages.text: The handler would now own row keys and paging as well as export behavior; a storage layout change would alter the use case.
A per-table repository exposes the storage split; the caller would have to reconstruct session meaning and order.
That moves query vocabulary and paging details into the caller, so it does not protect the board model from mapping changes.

feedback.reason: Keep the session lookup in a domain collection boundary because the use case needs a session and its committed ordered history, while the row key and page mechanics are explicitly changeable.

options.text: Have the export handler compose SQL against event rows and assemble the session itself.
Create a repository for every event table and have the handler join their returned records.
Pass a database-shaped filter and sort expression through a generic repository to the handler.
Use a session query for committed history in order; hide row keys and paging in the adapter.

questions.prompt: In a shared whiteboard application, a session host closes a board and exports its history. Each export must use the committed event sequence for one session; callers also need to list sessions by workspace. Board events are stored as rows whose keys and paging rules may change. What should the application depend on for session lookup?

constraints: The conversation has one current owner, a response deadline, and escalation history.
The endpoint queries open cases for one team from a large indexed case set.
Measured full-table materialization exceeds the endpoint’s 200 ms p95 target.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The repository exposes the conversation query and mapping boundary; the measured retrieval budget, not a general rule that every query must use a custom repository, rules out loading all cases here.
details.errorCorrection: A full load would materialize about 250,000 conversations and misses the stated 200 ms p95 target; the indexed team/open retrieval is the supported path for this endpoint.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A repository can present the persisted conversations like a collection and provide the named team query, while the persistence adapter joins the separate rows.
details.scenarioApplication: Here the alternative table repositories expose the storage decomposition, and the generic filter leaks SQL-like vocabulary; neither returns the domain unit needed by the escalation.
details.transfer: When mapping changes without changing the business query, preserve the domain query and change only its adapter.

messages.text: The handler would need to know the persistence split and would return a record shape instead of the conversation the rule operates on.
That preserves table boundaries as the public contract; it leaves the caller to rebuild which rows form a conversation.
This would materialize the full 250,000-row set and exceed the endpoint’s stated 200 ms p95 budget.

feedback.reason: The caller asks for open conversations by team and then escalates a domain conversation; the collection contract can hide the separate owner/history rows without inventing a new state owner.

options.text: Join the ownership and history tables in the use-case handler, then pass the combined record to the escalation code.
Use a conversation collection with a team/open query; keep ownership/history mapping behind it.
Give each table a repository and let the handler coordinate their calls for every escalation.
Load every conversation into memory and filter by team in the domain layer.

questions.prompt: In a customer-support escalation desk, the lead escalates a conversation. A conversation may have one current owner, a response deadline, and a sequence of prior escalations; the application searches the open cases for one team. The database stores ownership and history separately. The open-case table has about 250,000 rows, the endpoint has a 200 ms p95 target, and measured full-table materialization exceeds that budget. Which contract should the escalation use case call?

constraints: Publishing must validate price and stock before visibility changes.
The catalog asks for visible listings by region; storage keeps price and stock separately.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The repository is justified by the domain query and separated mapping here, not by a rule that every table deserves a repository.
details.errorCorrection: Keep arbitrary read projections outside this boundary when they are display-only, but route state-changing publication through the domain listing contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The repository contract returns listings and supports the visible-by-region search; its adapter can join the price and stock tables.
details.scenarioApplication: In this case the UI needs a listing, not an ORM graph, and publishing must validate before setting visibility; exposing independent rows splits one rule among callers.
details.transfer: If a future catalog projection does not invoke a domain rule, it may use a read query; do not let that projection become the write contract.

messages.text: The controller would duplicate mapping and move the publish rule out of the domain operation.
Visibility depends on both values, so separate row access makes each caller responsible for the same domain rule.
That makes the presentation code depend on the current mapping graph rather than the listing contract.

feedback.reason: The source facts make listing visibility a domain rule across two stored values and give callers a domain-shaped query; a listing collection contract keeps that meaning outside table joins.

options.text: Have the catalog controller join price and stock rows and decide which listing becomes visible.
Expose independent price and stock repositories and require each caller to decide when a listing is visible.
Return the ORM entities to the catalog and let it traverse persistence navigation properties.
Keep price/stock publication and region search in a listing contract; map rows in persistence.

questions.prompt: In a regional produce marketplace, the seller publishes seasonal inventory. A listing is visible only after its price and available stock have been validated together. Catalog screens also ask for visible listings in a region, while the database keeps prices and stock in separate tables. Which access contract best fits the publishing and listing code?

constraints: Each split retains the original request identity and delivery promise.
A deterministic test seam is required; callers should not depend on the marketplace database.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Use a repository contract for this shared domain access. A process-wide cache is not required and would add lifecycle behavior absent from the scenario.
details.errorCorrection: Direct SQL or raw-record repositories make each caller repeat the mapping and can lose the original request relationship during a split.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A domain collection query can return the backordered request as one object even when fulfillment uses several vendor rows.
details.scenarioApplication: Both use cases can use the same seam in tests; split identity and delivery promise stay on the request instead of being recreated by each caller.
details.transfer: When two operations need the same domain query and persistence layout must stay private, keep the contract stable and vary the adapter.

messages.text: Both callers would duplicate the row mapping and split logic, so identity and promise rules could diverge.
The callers would still own the mapping from vendor records back to one original request and its promise.
That keeps table representation visible to both callers and forces them to reconstruct the same domain request.

feedback.reason: The two use cases need the same backordered-request query, while each split keeps one request identity and delivery promise. A domain collection contract lets both callers use that request without rebuilding its relationship from vendor rows.

options.text: Have each use case query vendor and request tables directly, then build split requests in the caller.
Create separate repositories for request rows and vendor rows and make each caller combine them.
Share one backordered-request collection query across both workflows; keep vendor rows behind it.
Return raw request and vendor records from a generic repository to keep the interface small.

questions.prompt: In a repair-parts marketplace, a fulfillment specialist splits one backordered request across vendors. Every split must retain the request identity and delivery promise. Two use cases need to find backordered requests, and tests must exercise them without the marketplace database. Which contract should both use cases depend on?

constraints: The plot ID is stable across a transfer.
The caller needs reservation lookup and pending approvals for a plot.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The domain contract is justified because the persistence model may vary independently. It does not require a custom repository for every simple stored value.
details.errorCorrection: A generic interface that accepts storage query strings would only hide the branch syntactically; callers would still depend on each persistence format.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The repository returns reservation objects and supports the approval query; the adapter maps relational rows or documents into that same domain contract.
details.scenarioApplication: Stable reservation identity and retained approval history rule out treating a transfer as a plot-key overwrite.
details.transfer: Keep persistence selection in composition/configuration and keep the use case expressed in reservation language.

messages.text: The business workflow would become responsible for deployment-specific persistence details and both branches could drift.
The use case needs the reservation and pending status; interpreting raw history rows in the caller leaks the mapping.
Storage query strings are precisely what must vary; putting them in the contract defeats the stated boundary.

feedback.reason: The reservation remains a domain object across transfer, while the store may change; callers should ask the collection contract for a reservation rather than choose its persistence format.

options.text: Keep reservation lookup in domain terms while the adapter changes from relational rows to documents.
Put relational and document-store branches in the steward workflow so it can select the current schema.
Return approval-history rows and let the steward infer the active reservation from their order.
Expose a generic repository that accepts storage-specific query strings so both adapters can share one interface.

questions.prompt: In a community garden tool, a steward transfers a plot reservation between gardeners. The reservation has an approval history and its plot ID never changes. A steward can look up one reservation or list pending approvals for a plot; the storage engine may later change from relational rows to documents. Which boundary should expose these operations?

constraints: The bundle price is derived from the current component prices and regional adjustment.
Operators search active bundles using region and status.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Use the repository for this domain query and save path. Keep a display-only aggregate projection separate if it does not own the price rule.
details.errorCorrection: A wide record or per-region subtype makes the storage shape control the domain contract without a stated behavioral variation.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The caller searches bundles by region and active state through a domain query; the adapter can combine bundle and component persistence shapes.
details.scenarioApplication: Calculate the price at the bundle/domain operation so every caller observes the same derived rule rather than reimplementing it in a screen.
details.transfer: When the relational or document representation changes, callers can continue to request the same bundle concept.

messages.text: That duplicates a price rule in a display caller and permits different callers to calculate different bundle values.
The callers would need to reconstruct the bundle from storage-specific pieces and apply the same domain calculation.
That couples the domain bundle contract to a particular schema and breaks when component storage changes.

feedback.reason: Bundle lookup and pricing are domain operations, while bundle and component rows have different shapes; the repository contract keeps that mapping out of the catalog callers.

options.text: Have the catalog screen read component rows and calculate the bundle price before saving.
Expose a repository per component table and a separate bundle-row repository to all callers.
Return one wide persistence record containing every regional component column.
Expose bundles as domain values and map component rows behind the persistence boundary.

questions.prompt: In a subscription packaging service, a catalog manager creates a regional bundle from existing components. The bundle price is derived from component prices plus a regional adjustment; operators search bundles by region and active status. Components and bundles have different stored shapes. Which access contract should the bundle use?

constraints: Capacity is computed from active reservations after expired holds are released.
The query is for reservations belonging to one charger, not raw reservation rows.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A domain collection boundary is useful where multiple stored records participate in a domain query; it should not be an excuse for an unrelated cache.
details.errorCorrection: Filtering raw rows in each caller would make expiration semantics vary; an unsupported background counter would add a new consistency contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The repository query returns active reservations for a charger and coordinates the domain lookup used by the expiry-aware release path.
details.scenarioApplication: The charger row cannot answer capacity alone because the reservation facts are stored separately.
details.transfer: Callers should depend on charger/reservation concepts while adapters own joins and persistence filters.

messages.text: That duplicates expiration and capacity logic in every handler and exposes both table layouts.
The prompt says reservations live separately and capacity is computed from them, so metadata alone is insufficient.
That makes callers interpret persistence status fields and risks inconsistent expiry handling.

feedback.reason: The use case needs active reservation objects and a consistent expiry rule from the domain boundary; the storage split should not make each caller assemble capacity.

options.text: Let the scheduling handler query charger and reservation tables and implement expiration on each call.
Use an availability query by aircraft type, with assignment joins kept behind the collection.
Read charger metadata and assume its stored capacity already reflects every active reservation.
Return reservation rows to each caller and let it filter status and expiry locally.

questions.prompt: In a fleet charging coordinator, an operator reserves a charger. The system must return active reservations for a charger and release expired ones before it offers capacity. Reservation records are stored separately from charger metadata. Which API boundary should the scheduling use case use?

constraints: The asset identifier stays fixed while descriptive values change.
The screen asks for the current descriptions by language.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Repositories can expose domain queries while hiding storage mapping; do not turn language selection into a new subtype hierarchy.
details.errorCorrection: Keeping the SQL join in the screen leaks normalization; returning the raw document leaks the current serialization shape.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The screen asks for an asset and descriptions by language through domain terms, not by column selection.
details.scenarioApplication: The merge replaces descriptions without replacing the asset. A snapshot-only identity or language-specific subtype would change facts not requested.
details.transfer: Transfer the same contract if descriptions move from normalized rows to embedded values.

messages.text: The screen would depend on the current normalization and column name rather than the asset description contract.
Language is a query criterion; the facts do not establish different asset behavior for each language.
That transfers mapping and localization rules to the UI and makes a schema change visible to the caller.

feedback.reason: The stable identifier and replaceable localized descriptions are separate domain facts; the asset collection contract can preserve identity while the adapter changes table layout.

options.text: Join the asset and description tables in the screen and select the language column directly.
Create a distinct asset subtype for every language and store the description on that subtype.
Expose the persistence document to the archivist and let the UI select fields from its current shape.
Expose lookup by asset and language, with normalized descriptions mapped behind the contract.

questions.prompt: In a photo archive, an archivist merges duplicate descriptions for one asset. Asset identity is stable, but descriptions can be replaced. A review screen needs the asset by stable ID and all current descriptions in a chosen language; the database may normalize descriptions into another table. Which interface should the screen call?

constraints: An approval is scoped by an explicit territory and expiry.
Audit queries list approvals for a work.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keep the collection boundary because the audit and approval use cases share the same domain criteria.
details.errorCorrection: Territory code is a domain value, while the join table is persistence mapping. The caller should not provide SQL fragments.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The domain query takes a work and territory and returns only approvals whose expiry satisfies the rule.
details.scenarioApplication: Treating any join row as an approval ignores expiry; making approval global ignores territory scope.
details.transfer: If the database later embeds territories, the domain query can remain the same.

messages.text: That can omit the expiry condition and puts the join-table representation in presentation code.
Territories are data values in this case, not distinct approval behavior requiring separate types.
That keeps the adapter hidden but still makes the rights caller depend on the storage query language.

feedback.reason: An approval must be queried with territory and expiry, so a domain collection contract can express the rights rule while its adapter handles join rows.

options.text: Make the audit screen join work and territory tables and treat any returned row as an approval.
Use domain approval criteria for work, territory, and expiry; keep the join mapping private.
Create a type per territory and put the expiry rule in each type.
Make callers pass territory-code SQL fragments to the repository.

questions.prompt: In a digital-rights tool, an analyst approves a use for one territory. The approval lookup must require both territory and expiry, and the audit screen lists approvals for a work. The database stores territory codes in a join table. Which contract keeps those queries in the rights domain?

constraints: Availability is determined from assignments plus battery specifications.
The screen searches by aircraft type before scheduling.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Use this interface for the scheduling decision, but do not infer a distributed locking or transaction guarantee from the query itself.
details.errorCorrection: Do not treat a search result as the authority for assignment state: the prompt makes assignment records part of availability, so callers should request the combined domain result.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The query accepts aircraft type and returns batteries not already assigned; its adapter can read the two stored shapes.
details.scenarioApplication: Letting a screen filter specifications locally duplicates the one-aircraft invariant; a process-local list lacks a stated freshness contract.
details.transfer: The repository hides how assignments and specifications are stored while preserving the domain meaning of “available battery.”

messages.text: That moves the single-assignment rule to a display caller and exposes both storage layouts.
Every caller would reimplement the same availability rule and could disagree about assignments.
The prompt identifies assignments as part of availability and provides no cache refresh or cross-process consistency contract.

feedback.reason: Availability depends on two persistence sets but is one domain query; the repository boundary returns available batteries without making the screen rebuild the rule.

options.text: Use a domain availability query by aircraft type; keep assignment joins in persistence.
Have the screen join assignment and specification tables and decide availability itself.
Return all specifications and ask each caller to remove assigned battery IDs.
Keep one process-wide list of free batteries and use it instead of the assignment records.

questions.prompt: In a drone maintenance planner, a battery can be assigned to only one aircraft at a time. The fleet screen searches available batteries by aircraft type, then schedules one. Assignments and battery specifications are stored separately. Which boundary should expose the available-battery query?

constraints: The send operation checks consent before external disclosure.
The clinic report needs domain referrals awaiting review.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A domain collection contract limits what the navigator depends on; it does not itself promise an external send transaction.
details.errorCorrection: The consent check belongs to the send decision, but raw consent columns stay unavailable to the navigator; the repository contract must return a consent-aware referral rather than expose those columns.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The repository query expresses “awaiting review for this clinic” and returns a referral domain object; the adapter resolves stored consent details.
details.scenarioApplication: Do not move consent decisions to each caller or a cache without a stated freshness rule.
details.transfer: Keep privacy policy in the domain operation and keep storage columns behind the adapter.

messages.text: That exposes sensitive persistence columns to the caller and risks reproducing the consent predicate differently.
The prompt does not state a freshness interval or allow an out-of-date consent decision.
That makes every caller responsible for enforcing the same disclosure boundary.

feedback.reason: Consent has to be checked at the domain send operation while the caller is forbidden from reading its storage columns; a domain repository can supply the required consent-aware referral.

options.text: Have the navigator read referral and consent tables directly before sending.
Copy consent into a long-lived referral cache and trust the copy for all sends.
Return raw referral and consent records from separate repositories for every caller to combine.
Expose consent-aware referral access without raw consent columns in caller code.

questions.prompt: In a clinic referral coordinator, the navigator checks consent before sending a referral externally. A report also lists referrals awaiting review for a clinic. Consent facts are stored separately from referral details, and the navigator must not read raw consent-table columns. Which access contract fits?

constraints: Completion history must retain the exact exercise and score-policy revisions.
The screen queries by stable attempt ID.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The repository hides the persistence split but preserves the immutable revision references; it does not need to store the whole item as a blob.
details.errorCorrection: A history read must follow the attempt’s recorded revision references; resolving the latest policy would rewrite the meaning of a completed score.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The completion repository offers a domain lookup by attempt ID and maps its stored attempt and revision rows together.
details.scenarioApplication: Using latest policy changes the historical meaning of the attempt; raw row mapping makes the UI responsible for that distinction.
details.transfer: When a domain object records a stable historical reference, make the collection query return that same reference.

messages.text: That couples the screen to the split storage model and can accidentally select the latest rather than recorded policy.
That contradicts the exact revision references captured when the completion was made.
That duplicates revision mapping in the caller and risks using mutable current policy instead of the recorded one.

feedback.reason: The attempt points to immutable revisions, so repository lookup by attempt identity must return those recorded references rather than resolve current policy.

options.text: Have the history screen join attempts and policies using their current database keys.
Load the completion by stable attempt ID with its exact recorded revisions.
Load the current exercise and policy and display them for any attempt.
Return raw rows and let the screen assemble the completion domain object.

questions.prompt: In a music practice tracker, the learner completes a timed exercise. A completion record points to the exact exercise revision and score policy. The history screen looks up one completion by stable attempt ID; storage may split attempts from policy revisions. Which API boundary should the screen use?

constraints: A decision records its reviewer and cannot bypass the required controls.
Reviewers need pending exceptions within an assigned category.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keep the repository query constrained to the category and pending status. The approval operation still enforces controls when a decision is made.
details.errorCorrection: Keep the pending-category query separate from the decision controls: the category scopes the queue, while the approval workflow still applies its required controls.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A domain collection query can return pending exception cases; the adapter reads the separate approval and category records.
details.scenarioApplication: The UI and arbitrary SQL alternatives move the policy predicate into callers; per-table repositories leave them to rebuild the case.
details.transfer: Use a domain collection boundary when the stored graph is not the contract the workflow should manipulate.

messages.text: The UI would own the approval predicate and could expose a case that has not passed controls.
The workflow would have to reconstruct pending cases from storage pieces instead of consuming a domain queue.
The caller needs a category-scoped domain queue; SQL filters leak storage semantics and can bypass the policy query.

feedback.reason: The pending queue is a domain query scoped by reviewer category, and approval controls belong to the workflow rather than the presentation join.

options.text: Have the reviewer UI join category and approval tables and decide which exceptions are pending.
Create one public repository per approval, reviewer, and category table.
Expose a generic repository that accepts arbitrary sort and filter SQL from reviewers.
Query pending exceptions by category in domain terms, leaving row mapping in the adapter.

questions.prompt: In a procurement approval queue, an exception must have an attributable decision and pass required controls. Reviewers need a queue of pending exceptions for their assigned category. Approvals and category assignments are separate records. Which access contract should the approval workflow use?

constraints: Annotation identity follows the stable segment rather than the recording offset.
The editor retrieves annotations by segment ID.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keep format-specific offsets in the mapper, not the editor. No new annotation subtype is required by the stated formats.
details.errorCorrection: Do not recalculate annotation identity from waveform offsets after recording replacement; the stated stable segment ID is the lookup identity.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The collection contract retrieves annotations by segment ID and preserves their identity across source replacement.
details.scenarioApplication: Offset-based lookup is invalidated by the explicit identity rule; recording-based IDs would make replacement change identity.
details.transfer: The domain query can survive a storage or recording-format change because it uses the stable segment association.

messages.text: Byte offsets are explicitly not the annotation identity; the screen would have to reverse-engineer the mapping.
That would change annotation identity even though the facts say stable segment IDs own it.
That makes the editor depend on the persistence representation and reintroduces the known offset mismatch.

feedback.reason: The stable segment ID is the domain association; a persistence mapper can translate the separate waveform offsets without exposing them to the editor.

options.text: Have the editor read offset rows and adjust each annotation after replacement.
Key all annotations only by the current recording file and rewrite their IDs after each replacement.
Retrieve by stable segment identity; translate waveform offsets behind the collection.
Return database rows so the editor can infer segment identity from current offsets.

questions.prompt: In a podcast production desk, an editor replaces a source recording. Annotations attach to stable segment IDs, not byte offsets, and the editor searches annotations by segment. The database stores waveform offsets in a separate table. Which contract should the editor use?

constraints: Every grant points to its approval and expiry.
Auditors search active grants by principal.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An active grant query may take a time input, but its contract should not expose database keys or create role subclasses for data variants.
details.errorCorrection: An active-grant query must evaluate the grant’s approval and expiry together; a principal copy or caller-side joins would create a second interpretation of those facts.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The repository exposes the same grant collection to lookup and audit callers while keeping key translation private.
details.scenarioApplication: A second principal copy would add synchronization, while per-caller joins would duplicate the active predicate.
details.transfer: Use domain criteria in the repository API and adapt storage-specific keys behind it.

messages.text: That duplicates the time and approval predicates and risks inconsistent access reports.
The prompt does not define synchronization or a second authoritative copy for active grants.
That leaks row keys into the audit caller instead of using principal/time domain criteria.

feedback.reason: The audit needs the active-grant domain view with its approval link and expiry, although the database stores those facts under separate keys.

options.text: Query active grants by principal and time through a grant-domain collection.
Let each auditor query the two tables and decide whether a grant is active.
Copy active roles into a principal record whenever a grant changes.
Pass database key and time filters from the audit screen into a generic repository.

questions.prompt: In a permissions review service, a temporary role is granted only after a named approval and expires at a stated time. Auditors search active grants for one principal. Approval and grant rows use different storage keys. Which contract should the audit and grant workflows share?

constraints: A seal is attached to an exact immutable revision.
A notary lists sealed revisions by document ID.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The contract keeps the exact revision visible and storage joins private, without promising a particular blob-store implementation.
details.errorCorrection: Resolve the seal’s exact revision reference, not the document’s latest revision; that preserves what was signed while hiding the two-store join.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The collection can list sealed revisions by document and resolve the referenced bytes through its adapter.
details.scenarioApplication: Loading the latest revision would silently change what was sealed; returning seal rows alone separates the linked domain facts.
details.transfer: When a persisted object spans metadata and payload stores, expose the linked domain object if callers reason about that link.

messages.text: That couples the signing path to the storage split and can confuse the exact revision with the current document.
A seal points to an immutable exact revision, not whichever revision is latest at read time.
That leaves each caller to maintain the seal-to-revision relationship from two storage channels.

feedback.reason: The immutable revision reference is part of the seal domain object, so the signing workflow should not recreate that association from storage keys.

options.text: Have the signing handler load revision bytes and seal rows itself before returning a result.
Resolve the document ID to the latest revision whenever a seal is read.
Return seal rows only and make callers retrieve revision bytes independently.
Return the exact sealed revision by document ID; map seal and bytes behind the contract.

questions.prompt: In a document notarization service, a seal refers to one immutable document revision. A notary may list sealed revisions by document ID, but the database stores seals and revision bytes separately. Which contract should the signing workflow depend on?

constraints: A payout release is tied to a settled order and must not create a second release for the same operation.
Audit lookup is by seller and settlement window.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The contract is limited to the specified settled-order idempotency; it does not assert a distributed exactly-once protocol.
details.errorCorrection: Apply the settled-order duplicate rule at the persisted payout operation; caller prechecks and a process-local set do not represent the shared release contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The repository operation can enforce the stated idempotent release key and provide seller/window domain lookup.
details.scenarioApplication: A caller precheck or process-local set cannot replace one shared persisted operation contract across the described callers.
details.transfer: Keep persistence mapping behind the domain boundary and keep the guarantee no broader than the scenario states.

messages.text: A caller-side precheck cannot be the shared domain contract and duplicates the idempotency decision.
The scenario gives no process lifetime or cross-instance guarantee for such a set.
That requires callers to reconstruct settlement and payout meaning from storage details.

feedback.reason: The release and audit paths share payout-domain semantics, while the settlement and payout rows are only the current representation of those facts.

options.text: Let every caller query settlement and payout tables before attempting a release.
Expose payout release and seller/window lookup through a domain contract.
Use a process-local set of released order IDs as the only duplicate guard.
Expose raw order and payout rows through a generic data gateway.

questions.prompt: In a marketplace payout service, each release is idempotent for a settled order. Operations can inspect payouts by seller and settlement window; order settlement facts and payout rows are stored separately. Which interface should release and audit callers use?

constraints: The notice history is ordered by when changes became effective.
The query is scoped to route and service day.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keep effective-time ordering as a domain query rule; do not mistake the database insertion sequence for the stated order.
details.errorCorrection: Use effective time for the notice order and retain prior notices; row insertion order and a latest-value snapshot answer different questions.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The repository returns notice objects in the specified effective order for a route and day.
details.scenarioApplication: Ordering by row creation or keeping only the latest value would violate the history contract.
details.transfer: If route and notice tables are later reorganized, the same route-history contract can remain stable.

messages.text: Creation time is not the stated effective order, and the screen would depend on the storage join.
The scenario requires a notice history, so a latest-value snapshot cannot answer the audit query.
That moves route association and effective-order semantics into every consumer.

feedback.reason: The operator needs route-scoped notice history ordered by effective time; a domain collection query expresses both while hiding route/notice storage records.

options.text: Have the operator screen join route and notice tables and order by the database row creation time.
Keep only the latest platform value on the route and discard prior notices.
Return raw notice rows and let each client reconstruct the route and effective sequence.
Query route/day notices in effective-time order; keep row sequence mechanics in persistence.

questions.prompt: In a public-transit disruption board, passengers must receive platform changes in effective order. Operators also search the notice history for a route and service day; storage uses separate route and notice records. Which contract should the operator workflow call?

constraints: Door authorization reads badge active/revoked state.
Audit export is allowed to lag after revocation succeeds.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The premise separates an immediate access rule from a lag-tolerant report, so expanding the boundary to all doors or reports is unnecessary.
details.errorCorrection: If door authorization still reads an active value after success, the stated revocation result is false even if an audit row exists.
details.mechanismOrProperty: One badge state is the consistency unit for this command; an export can consume its later update without joining that unit.
details.scenarioApplication: For this badge, the immediate door decision reads access state; it does not wait for the delayed audit export.
details.transfer: Use the same rule when a command has one immediate decision and a separate projection with an explicit lag budget.

messages.text: A door could still grant access after the command reports success, which violates the stated authorization boundary.
The door configurations and lag-tolerant audit do not participate in the one-badge revocation invariant; site-wide scope adds unrelated contention.
The export is explicitly allowed to lag, so it cannot be the authority for an immediate access decision.
The facts require a coherent badge access decision, not a lock over independent readers and a lag-tolerant export.

feedback.reason: The command may report success only after authorization no longer sees the badge as active, while audit export has an explicit lag allowance. Keep the access state together and let the audit projection follow.

options.text: Commit revocation to the audit log first and let each door cache learn about it on its next refresh.
Put every badge, door configuration, and audit export for the site into one aggregate.
Commit the badge’s revocation and access state in one boundary.
Let the audit export decide whether the badge is revoked when a door asks for authorization.
Require a distributed lock across every door and audit consumer before revocation can succeed.

questions.prompt: At a smart-building site, the facilities team revokes a badge after an employee leaves. The door policy must never grant access from a badge record that still says active after the revocation command reports success. A separate audit export may lag by a minute. Which consistency boundary fits?

constraints: The label request identifies one approved shipment revision.
Printing status may be retried without changing that revision.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Only the revision-to-label meaning is coupled here; printer attempts do not become part of the shipment invariant.
details.errorCorrection: Reading current mutable fields or assembling rows in the screen can silently substitute a different address for the one named by the request.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The request should carry an immutable revision identity so the worker can render the approved address even if a later revision exists.
details.scenarioApplication: The print worker follows the revision named by the operator’s approval, even if another address revision is later created.
details.transfer: When asynchronous work must represent a chosen revision, persist that reference instead of expanding the aggregate to include worker mechanics.

messages.text: A later edit could make the label differ from the revision the request approved.
Printer retries do not change the approved shipment revision, so grouping them with shipment data couples independent work.
A retry is for the same named revision; making a new shipment for each attempt changes shipment identity.
That leaves the revision association to a caller and can mix fields from different approved versions.

feedback.reason: The approved revision is the value the label request promises to represent, but a printer retry changes only delivery status. Preserve that reference and keep retry bookkeeping separate.

options.text: Have the printer read whichever address is currently on the shipment when its worker runs.
Put the shipment, printer queue, and every retry counter in one aggregate.
Create a new shipment aggregate for every print attempt.
Let the operator screen assemble label fields from separate address and shipment tables.
Bind each label request to its approved shipment revision.

questions.prompt: After an address correction, a shipping operator approves a shipment revision and requests a package label. Each label must show the address from the approved revision named by that request. Printing status can be retried independently. What should share the consistency boundary?

constraints: Overlapping bookings for one room cannot exceed 20 attendees.
Cancellation fees do not affect occupancy and are calculated later.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The scenario requires a valid confirmed schedule, not eventual repair after an over-capacity commitment.
details.errorCorrection: Checking only the booking misses concurrent occupants; a tenant-wide lock includes rooms whose reservations cannot affect this capacity rule.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The room-level boundary can compare the incoming attendees with its current overlapping reservations before accepting the move.
details.scenarioApplication: A move consumes capacity in the destination room only for bookings whose times overlap the moved rehearsal.
details.transfer: Choose the smallest consistency boundary that can evaluate all values participating in the invariant.

messages.text: A single booking can fit while the combined overlapping bookings exceed room capacity.
The invariant is per room and overlapping time; unrelated rooms do not contribute to the capacity count.
The fee is explicitly independent of occupancy and runs later; it cannot arbitrate whether the destination room has space.
That leaves a confirmed schedule violating the immediate capacity invariant.

feedback.reason: The destination decision depends on the combined overlapping bookings for that room, not only the moved booking. The later fee calculation has no role in whether the room can accept it.

options.text: Check only that the moved booking has at most 20 attendees, then accept it.
Arbitrate the room’s overlapping reservations at its capacity boundary.
Lock all rehearsal bookings for every room in the tenant before any move.
Recalculate and commit the cancellation fee before changing room occupancy.
Accept the move and repair over-capacity schedules during the nightly report.

questions.prompt: A rehearsal scheduler moves a booking between rooms. Each room has a fixed capacity of 20; two overlapping bookings may not exceed it. A customer cancellation fee is calculated later and does not affect room occupancy. Which boundary should arbitrate the move?

constraints: The maintenance mode used by command validation.
Temperature readings are read-only and do not enable movement.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The scope is one exhibit’s command rule, not a transaction over all exhibits or telemetry storage.
details.errorCorrection: A disabled screen button cannot protect a controller that accepts commands from other callers; checking temperature substitutes the wrong fact.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The state boundary needs the mode used to accept or reject a movement, while telemetry can be recorded without changing command eligibility.
details.scenarioApplication: The arm command is accepted or rejected using the exhibit’s current maintenance mode; a temperature observation is not that mode.
details.transfer: Keep the state that governs an immediate command decision with that decision; separate observations that do not participate in it.

messages.text: Temperature is explicitly not the signal that permits or rejects arm movement.
The guard applies to one exhibit arm; unrelated exhibits and read-only readings do not join that invariant.
That applies the guard after the unsafe action instead of rejecting the command while maintenance is active.
The premise is a controller command rule; a UI-only check does not govern other command callers.

feedback.reason: The controller must evaluate the maintenance state at the same decision point as the movement command. Temperature telemetry is not part of that guard and can remain an independent feed.

options.text: Infer maintenance mode from the most recent temperature reading before each movement command.
Group every exhibit and all incoming telemetry in one state boundary.
Move the arm and then record that maintenance was active.
Keep maintenance mode and the arm-command guard in the exhibit state.
Let the technician’s screen disable the movement button and trust that no other caller can send the command.

questions.prompt: An exhibit controller enters maintenance mode before a technician opens a panel. While maintenance is active, commands that move the display arm must be rejected. Read-only temperature telemetry may continue arriving independently. Which state belongs together for command validation?

constraints: Retirement stops new assignments but preserves the lesson identity for existing progress.
The retirement report is a nightly rebuild.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This operation changes one catalog lifecycle fact. It does not require a bulk edit of learners or synchronous report regeneration.
details.errorCorrection: Rewriting progress or changing its ID would contradict the explicit continuation rule; waiting for a report leaves assignment eligibility stale.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The lesson lifecycle state can close future assignment while leaving the stable lesson identity and existing progress intact.
details.scenarioApplication: Learner progress continues to reference the same lesson while the catalog stops offering it to new assignments.
details.transfer: Keep lifecycle state with the entity whose future use it governs; preserve historical references when the scenario requires them.

messages.text: Existing learners may continue and progress refers to the stable lesson ID, so deletion breaks the stated relationship.
Progress is allowed to continue under the same identity, and the report is rebuilt later; neither needs to be rewritten for retirement.
A nightly report is not the stated authority for allowing new course assignments.
That changes the stable identity that existing progress is required to keep.

feedback.reason: Retirement changes whether new assignments may select the lesson, not which lesson existing progress refers to. The nightly report is a downstream projection and does not belong in that state change.

options.text: Retire assignment availability while keeping the lesson’s stable ID.
Delete the lesson row and rewrite each learner’s progress to a replacement lesson.
Include every learner progress record and nightly report in the lesson retirement transaction.
Wait for the next report rebuild to decide whether new assignments can use the lesson.
Create a new lesson ID for retirement and redirect old progress to it.

questions.prompt: A learning library retires a lesson from new course assignments. Learners who already started it may continue, and their progress uses the lesson’s stable ID. The retirement report is rebuilt nightly. Which change should be atomic with retirement?

constraints: The close marker separates the exported event sequence.
Email notification may be delayed.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Only one session’s ordered history participates in this decision; the email provider is a separate effect.
details.errorCorrection: Current events at worker time are not equivalent to events committed before close, and process-local markers cannot define a durable export boundary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The session decision identifies the last included event; the worker can use that fixed boundary even when notification is delayed.
details.scenarioApplication: The persisted close marker defines the event cutoff that the delayed export worker must use.
details.transfer: For a delayed consumer, store the domain boundary it must honor instead of relying on the caller’s memory or timing.

messages.text: Email delivery does not define the session’s committed event boundary.
That ignores the explicit close marker and can change the export after the session was closed.
The boundary is one session’s event sequence; unrelated boards do not contribute to it.
A delayed worker needs the committed boundary, not a marker that disappears with the host process.

feedback.reason: The export is defined by the session sequence around its persisted close marker; email timing is independent. Persist the marker and sequence boundary before asking a worker to export.

options.text: Wait for the email provider to accept a notification before deciding which events belong in the export.
Export the latest events whenever the worker runs, including events committed after close.
Commit the close marker with the session event-sequence boundary.
Lock every board session while one session closes and exports.
Keep the close marker only in the host process and let the export worker infer it later.

questions.prompt: A whiteboard session host closes a board for export. The export must contain all events committed before the close marker and none committed afterward. An email notification may be delayed. Which values must be decided together at close?

constraints: Owner and response deadline form one accepted escalation result.
The activity feed may update afterward.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The scenario couples two fields on one conversation, not every conversation sharing a queue.
details.errorCorrection: A separate write can expose a mismatched pair, and a lagging feed cannot safely reconstruct the authoritative state.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Treat the paired values as one conversation transition and let the feed consume the accepted result.
details.scenarioApplication: The conversation is observed as escalated only when its owner and response deadline reflect the same transition.
details.transfer: When the caller observes a paired state change as one result, keep those values within the same consistency decision.

messages.text: The conversation could temporarily show the new owner with the old deadline even though the prompt requires one accepted result.
The feed may lag, so it cannot be the authority for the accepted conversation state.
The paired owner/deadline change concerns one conversation; the whole queue does not participate in that transition.
That exposes a partially accepted transition to other callers, contrary to the stated same-result requirement.

feedback.reason: The command has one visible result: a new owner paired with its response deadline. A lagging activity feed can record that transition afterward without serving as its authority.

options.text: Change the owner now and recompute the deadline in a later job.
Let the activity feed reconstruct the current owner and deadline for each caller.
Group every conversation in the specialist queue into one aggregate before any escalation.
Have the escalation screen issue separate owner and deadline writes and retry whichever fails.
Commit owner and deadline as one conversation transition.

questions.prompt: An escalation desk raises a conversation to a specialist queue. The assigned owner and response deadline must change in the same accepted escalation; a separate activity feed may update afterward. Which boundary should own acceptance?

constraints: Price and stock must pass both checks before the listing becomes searchable.
Search indexing may lag after publication.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The consistency scope is one listing; no fact requires a transaction across every seller listing or the index.
details.errorCorrection: An eventually updated index cannot enforce a pre-publication condition, and checking only price omits one required value.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The listing transition owns the joint price/stock check; search can catch up without reopening that validity decision.
details.scenarioApplication: The listing becomes searchable only after its own price and stock values satisfy the publication checks.
details.transfer: Separate a state transition’s required facts from a read projection that may be refreshed afterward.

messages.text: The index is allowed to lag and is not the authority that prevents an invalid listing from becoming published.
The prompt requires both values before publication, so a valid price alone is insufficient.
Only one listing’s two checks participate in this decision; seller-wide and index state are separate.
The stated publication rule requires nonnegative stock, not a stale projected value.

feedback.reason: Publication depends on two current listing facts, while indexing is explicitly allowed to lag. Validate both before changing the listing’s published state and project the result later.

options.text: Publish first and let the search index reject listings with invalid price or stock.
Validate current price and stock in the listing publication transition.
Check positive price but defer stock validation until the first purchase.
Place every listing, seller account, and search index document in one aggregate.
Treat the latest stock projection as sufficient even if the listing’s current stock is negative.

questions.prompt: A marketplace publishes a seasonal listing. A listing is searchable only when its price is positive and available stock is nonnegative; the search index can lag after publication. Which boundary should decide publication?

constraints: Each child shipment retains the request ID and delivery promise.
Vendor confirmations may arrive independently and reporting combines them later.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The request identity is shared across the split; the external confirmations remain independently arriving facts.
details.errorCorrection: Creating unrelated child request IDs breaks the stated association, while requiring all vendors to confirm invents cross-vendor atomicity.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The request transition records children linked to the parent; each vendor response updates its own confirmation state.
details.scenarioApplication: Each vendor child remains attached to the same parent request even though vendor acknowledgements arrive at different times.
details.transfer: When a business decision must preserve a parent relationship but collaborators respond independently, avoid grouping their entire lifecycles together.

messages.text: The vendors confirm independently, so waiting for all of them changes the stated workflow and creates a cross-vendor transaction.
That loses the original request identity the scenario explicitly requires every child to retain.
The view is built later from independent confirmations and is not the authority for the parent request identity.
Independent vendor confirmations and a later report do not need to change the identity-preserving split decision.

feedback.reason: The split plan must preserve one parent request identity and promise, but independent vendor confirmations do not form one synchronous outcome. Keep the plan decision local and let the report combine later confirmations.

options.text: Require every vendor to confirm before any split plan can be recorded.
Give each vendor child a new request identity and copy the delivery promise into it.
Let the combined reporting view own the split plan and decide whether the request exists.
Commit the split plan under the parent request’s identity and promise.
Put vendor confirmation states and reporting rows inside one request aggregate.

questions.prompt: A fulfillment specialist splits a backordered request across vendors. The child shipments keep the original request ID and promised delivery date; each vendor can confirm independently. A reporting view combines confirmations later. What should remain one domain transition?

constraints: The plot has at most one active reservation throughout an accepted transfer.
Approval history is append-only and may be exported later.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Only the reservation slot for this plot is coupled; the append-only export can lag.
details.errorCorrection: Changing one record without checking the slot can create a duplicate; two independent commits can expose the forbidden empty interval.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The plot-scoped reservation decision must arbitrate the old-to-new assignment together.
details.scenarioApplication: The plot’s active reservation changes from the former gardener to the new one without exposing an empty or duplicate slot.
details.transfer: When uniqueness is defined across several records, put the arbitration at the smallest boundary that can see those records.

messages.text: The field update alone does not prevent two active reservations for the same plot.
The invariant is scoped to the transferred plot; other plots cannot create a second active reservation for it.
The history export is later and does not decide whether the plot has exactly one active assignment.
That exposes a state with no active reservation despite the accepted transfer’s stated continuity rule.

feedback.reason: The transfer’s correctness is defined at the plot slot: accepted state must have one active gardener rather than a duplicate or gap. Exporting approval history does not participate in that invariant.

options.text: Transfer the plot’s active-reservation slot in one coordinated change.
Change only the reservation’s gardener field without checking the plot’s active slot.
Lock every plot in the garden while transferring one reservation.
Wait for the approval-history export to finish before updating the active reservation.
End the old reservation, commit, and create the new one in a later independent request.

questions.prompt: A garden steward transfers a reservation from one gardener to another. The plot has one active reservation; the transfer must leave either the old gardener or the new gardener assigned, never both and never neither. Approval history is append-only and may be exported later. What state must be coordinated for transfer?

constraints: An issued quote references exact component revisions and its adjustment.
Later component prices do not alter an issued quote.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This boundary preserves one quote’s historical inputs; it does not require all catalog prices to share its lifecycle.
details.errorCorrection: Reading live prices or looking up the adjustment later would replace values that the prompt says are fixed on the issued quote.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Treat the quote as the immutable record of those exact inputs, while current product pricing evolves independently.
details.scenarioApplication: The issued quote remains tied to the component revisions and adjustment selected when that quote was made.
details.transfer: Keep a priced decision’s exact inputs with that decision when later source values are allowed to change.

messages.text: That would change an issued quote after the fact, contrary to the fixed revision and adjustment facts.
An issued quote is fixed by its referenced revisions; unrelated products do not contribute to that quote.
The quote itself includes a fixed adjustment, so a later lookup could substitute another value.
The region supplies a value used in the quote; the prompt does not require distinct bundle behavior or all historical prices.

feedback.reason: The quote’s promised amount is tied to both its referenced component revisions and the fixed adjustment. Later catalog changes must not recalculate that already-issued result.

options.text: Recalculate every issued quote from the latest component prices whenever it is read.
Include every regional product price in one aggregate so no quote can become stale.
Commit component revisions and the adjustment in an immutable quote.
Store component revisions now and look up the regional adjustment only when checkout occurs.
Create a different bundle type for each region and embed all component price history in it.

questions.prompt: A packaging service creates a regional bundle from component products. At quote time, the bundle stores the exact component revisions and a fixed regional adjustment; later component price changes must not rewrite an issued quote. Which values must the quote preserve together?

constraints: The charger has no overlapping active reservations.
Expired holds are excluded before accepting a new reservation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The rule is scoped to one charger and its active holds, not every charger or a separate maintenance index.
details.errorCorrection: Checking one reservation misses competing intervals, and waiting for nightly cleanup contradicts the explicit expiry rule.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The charger-scoped schedule can evaluate the complete interval set needed for non-overlap.
details.scenarioApplication: A reservation is checked against every active interval on that charger after expired holds are excluded.
details.transfer: An invariant over a set requires the decision boundary to see the relevant set, but not unrelated data.

messages.text: A different active reservation may occupy the same interval, so a single-record check misses the invariant.
The index describes maintenance notes, not the active reservation intervals named by the rule.
The non-overlap rule is per charger; unrelated intervals on other chargers do not affect this slot.
The prompt says an expired hold frees its interval before a new reservation is accepted.
